docs.title: Cirrus
docs.text:
Cirrus is a STAC-based geospatial processing framework built on serverless AWS infrastructure. It supplies the parts that are the same in every processing pipeline — queueing, workflow execution, state tracking, publishing — so you can focus on your processing code. And because inputs and outputs are STAC items, results are immediately ready for ingest into a STAC catalog or use in another Cirrus workflow.

Cirrus is proven in production. The pipelines that populate Earth Search, Element 84's public STAC catalog of open Earth observation data, run on Cirrus for both daily ingest and full-catalog reprocessing.

docs.text: Unless otherwise listed, the changes for this release were part of PR #369.

docs.title: ⚠️ Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Payload bucket reorganization: all payload S3 keys are now organized under a configurable root prefix (default cirrus). Input and output payloads are stored per-execution at {root_prefix}/executions/{payload_id}/{execution_id}/input.json and output.json. Temporary objects (oversized payloads, batch I/O, invalid payloads) are stored under {root_prefix}/tmp/.
  • Management CLI command get-payload renamed get-input-payload
  • Management CLI command get-payloads renamed get-input-payloads
  • StateDB and EventDB, and thus the API responses, switch COMPLETED state name to SUCCEEDED
  • Workflow event type ALREADY_COMPLETED renamed to ALREADY_SUCCEEDED
  • Workflow events payload_url field renamed to input_payload_url; a new output_payload_url field is included on SUCCEEDED and ALREADY_SUCCEEDED events
  • Workflow event type CLAIMED and some FAILED events now do not include a payload_url at all (these are emitted prior to the payload upload to S3 so the URL is not actually valid)

If using cirrus as a library, be aware of the following:

  • StateDB.get_dbitem() now raises a PayloadNotFoundError instead of returning None when no item matches the supplied ID
  • StateDB.set_completed() renamed to set_succeeded()
  • StateDB.dbitem_to_item() changed from a classmethod to an instance method
  • StateDB.payload_id_to_url() and StateDB.payload_key_to_url() removed; use StateDB.payload_id_to_input_payload_url() or StateDB.payload_id_to_output_payload_url() instead
  • StateDB.payload_id_to_bucket_key() removed
  • Standalone functions get_payload_bucket() and get_state_db() removed from cirrus.lib.statedb
  • StateDB item representation changed: catalog field renamed to input_payload_url; new output_payload_url and claimed_at fields added
  • PayloadManager.upload_to_s3() static method removed; use PayloadBucket methods instead
  • PayloadNotFoundError moved from cirrus.management.exceptions to cirrus.exceptions
  • NoExecutionsError removed from cirrus.management.exceptions; replaced by ExecutionNotFoundError in cirrus.exceptions
  • Deployment.yield_payloads() removed; replaced by Deployment.yield_workflow_items() and Deployment.yield_input_payloads()
  • Deployment.get_execution_arn() no longer accepts an arn keyword argument; it now takes only payload_id as a positional parameter
  • Deployment.fetch_payload() signature changed: rerun parameter replaced with direction parameter ("input" or "output")
  • CloudFormation templates now include a new PayloadRootPrefix parameter (defaults to cirrus); the payload bucket has a lifecycle rule to expire objects under {root_prefix}/tmp/ after 10 days

docs.title: Migration notes
docs.text:
We've added a new management CLI command migrate, which will migrate all state database records to the new format while also copying all possible input payloads and output payloads into the new locations in the payloads bucket. This tool uses a DynamoDB table scan to process all records. The operation is idempotent, but will do a full scan every run.

Input payloads will not get copied into place if they were URL reference payloads. Output payloads will only be written for executions within the last 90 days per the step functions history retention limit.

Run this command after deploying this v2 release to ensure your state database and payload organization is consistent with the latest changes. Note that S3 objects are only ever copied, not moved: clean up of items outside the new organization tree is left to the user.

With the new payload bucket organization, only one lifecycle policy is required to clean up temp objects (oversized payloads between steps, batch input/output, etc.). Set that lifecycle policy on the /{root_prefix}/tmp/ key prefix, where {root_prefix} is the value of CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_ROOT_PREFIX (default cirrus).

docs.title: ⚠️ Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Serverless version >=3 is now required per the addition of a DLQ for the update-state events (#182).

Note that upgrading to serverless v3 changes the type of EventBridge Rules resources. In testing we found that the existing update-state rule needed to be deleted by CloudFormation before adding the new rule. Manually deleting the existing rule before deployment was not sufficient, as CloudFormation ended up removing the new rule after it was created.

In short, the simplest thing to do after upgrading serverless is to deploy twice, once with update-state disabled and again with it re-enabled.

To disable it, it is easiest to run this from your project root:

mkdir functions/update-state
echo "description: temporarily disabled" > functions/update-state/definition.yml

Then, run the deploy as normal. Once that is complete, remove the update-state override:

rm -r functions/update-state

Deploy again and update-state and its event should be re-created successfully.

Note that state tracking/workflow chaining will be broken between the first deploy and the second. It is strongly recommended to do this only when your pipelines are not processing workflows.

  • The process SNS topic has been removed (#169). All feeder/scripts/etc. should use the process SQS queue directly. If project needs require the SNS topic for migration or other use, the removed configuration can be reintroduced by adding the following CloudFormation template to your project:
# cloudformation/sns.yml
Resources:
  ProcessTopic:
    Type: "AWS::SNS::Topic"
    Properties:
      TopicName: "#{AWS::StackName}-process"
  ProcessQueuePolicy:
    Type: AWS::SQS::QueuePolicy
    Properties:
      Queues:
        - !Ref ProcessQueue
      PolicyDocument:
        Statement:
          - Sid: allow-sqs-sendmessage
            Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              AWS: "*"
            Action: SQS:SendMessage
            Resource: !GetAtt ProcessQueue.Arn
            Condition:
              ArnEquals:
                aws:SourceArn:
                  - !Ref ProcessTopic
  ProcessQueueSubsciption:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Subscription
    Properties:
      Endpoint: !GetAtt ProcessQueue.Arn
      Protocol: sqs
      Region: "#{AWS::Region}"
      TopicArn: !Ref ProcessTopic

Outputs:
  CirrusQueueSnsArn:
    Value: !Ref ProcessTopic

• Serverless versions through 3.x now supported. Minimum serverless of 2.3.0 is now required per pseudo parameters now being parsed within cirrus, rather than via the serverless-pseudo-parameters plugin. (#139)

Tested package.json dependency versions:

  "serverless": "~3.18.0",
  "serverless-python-requirements": "~5.4.0",
  "serverless-step-functions": "~3.7.0",
  "serverless-iam-roles-per-function": "~3.2.0"

Note that upgrading to serverless v3 changes the type of EventBridge Rules resources. In testing we found that the existing update-state rule needed to be deleted by CloudFormation before adding the new rule. Manually deleting the existing rule before deployment was not sufficient, as CloudFormation ended up removing the new rule after it was created.

In short, the simplest thing to do after upgrading serverless is to deploy twice, once with update-state disabled and again with it re-enabled.

To disable it, it is easiest to run this from your project root:

mkdir functions/update-state
echo "description: temporarily disabled" > functions/update-state/definition.yml

Then, run the deploy as normal. Once that is complete, remove the update-state override:

rm -r functions/update-state

Deploy again and update-state and its event should be re-created successfully.

Note that state tracking/workflow chaining will be broken between the first deploy and the second. It is strongly recommended to do this only when your pipelines are not processing workflows.

  • All lambda component definitions need the handler populated if not already. Previously cirrus was defaulting handler to lambda_function.lambda_handler if it were omitted. Now the default lambda definition.yml includes handler: lambda_function.lambda_handler, allowing users to remove it if not compatible with their needs (i.e., specifying a container image). (#139)

  • S3 buckets Data and Payload are no longer defined as builtins. Projects that do not otherwise define their required S3 buckets should ensure they have both of these buckets defined in their cloudformation resource templates. The previously-default configuration looks like this (#147):

# cloudformation/s3.yml
Resources:
  # Main data bucket
  Data:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: "#{AWS::StackName}-data"
  # Bucket for storing input catalogs
  Payloads:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: "#{AWS::StackName}-payloads"
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          - ExpirationInDays: 10
            Prefix: batch/
            Status: Enabled
          - ExpirationInDays: 10
            Prefix: payloads/
            Status: Enabled

Note that if a bucket not part your existing cirrus project already exists with the same name specified here, cloudformation will fail. Ensure you are only using these default bucket names if your project was previously relying on these built-in resources.

  • Batch IAM role best practices have changed, and some builtin roles have changed or been removed. See #149 for additional context. In summary:

  • Do not specify the service role on batch compute environments. The builtin BatchServiceRole has been removed from cirrus. The default role automatically provided by AWS automatically is sufficient.

    Note that existing compute environments have to be deleted and recreated using the new service role, as CloudFormation seems to be unable to update the service role and will instead leave all compute environments that have simply had the service role removed in an invalid state.

  • All non-standard permissions have been removed from the BatchInstanceRole. If you have been overriding that role with custom permissions review the new BatchJobRole and override with any further permissions instead. Better yet, create a unique role per batch task based on the BatchJobRole.

  • When using BatchJobRole or a custom role per batch task, ensure it is specified on the job definition as the ContainerProperties JobRoleArn.

  • The cli command to create new tasks now uses -t/--type to specify the task type, instead of --has-batch/--no-batch and --has-lambda/--no-lambda. -t/--type has no default value and is required. It can be specified multiple times in the case of a task that uses both batch and lambda. (#123)

• lambda python_requirements renamed pythonRequirements and nested under lambda key in lambda definition; requirements listed under include key

  pythonRequirements:
    include:
      - 'a_package==1.2.3'
  • now using cirrus-lib>=0.6.0; see the breaking changes in the 0.6.0 release and update lambda handlers accordingly
  • all CloudFormation templates move from resources/ and outputs/ to cloudformation/
  • the custom compute environment resources have been removed, so batch jobs using those need to declare their own; switching to batch tasks is recommended
  • global IAM permissions have been removed; audit all IAM permissions and declare them as needed in the corresponding component's definition.yml
  • queue topic renamed process

  • global env vars have been cleaned up; make sure all lambdas/batch jobs have the vars they require

Some of the above do not apply unless cirrus.yml is recreated from the new default template. It is recommended to delete cirrus.yml, rerun cirrus init, and then replace all custom cirrus.yml content that is still required.

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
Get uv. Then:

git clone https://github.com/cirrus-geo/cirrus-geo.git
cd cirrus-geo
uv sync --extra cli --python <python_version>

Run pre-commit install to enable the pre-commit configuration:

uv run pre-commit install

The pre-commit hooks will be run against all files during a git commit, or you can run it explicitly with:

uv run pre-commit run --all-files

If, for some reason, you wish to commit code that does not pass the pre-commit checks, this can be done with:

git commit -m "message" --no-verify

docs.title: Dependency management
docs.text:
Dependencies are defined in pyproject.toml:

  • [project.dependencies]: base application dependencies
  • [project.optional-dependencies.cli]: dependencies specific to the cli extra
  • [dependency-groups.dev]: development dependencies
  • [dependency-groups.docs]: dependencies for building docs

docs.title: Adding dependencies
docs.text:
To add a new base dependency:

uv add <package_name>

To add a development dependency:

uv add --group dev <package_name>

To add a documentation dependency:

uv add --group docs <package_name>

To add a CLI-specific dependency:

uv add --optional cli <package_name>

docs.title: Updating dependencies
docs.text:
To upgrade a specific package:

uv sync --upgrade-package <package_name>

To upgrade all dependencies:

uv sync --upgrade

docs.title: Installing all dependencies
docs.text:
To install all dependencies (base, dev, docs, and cli):

uv sync --all-groups --all-extras

docs.title: Python library
docs.text:
The cirrus-geo distribution installs the cirrus package, which has two parts. cirrus.lib is the library the five framework Lambda functions are built on: the payload model, the state database and payload bucket clients, workflow events, and logging. cirrus.management is the layer under the Cirrus CLI and needs the cli extra (pip install 'cirrus-geo[cli]').

Tasks mostly do not import either. A task is built on stac-task, and its only coupling to Cirrus is the payload it receives and returns. The places user code does reach for cirrus:

Need Import Notes Build or validate a payload in a feeder cirrus.lib.cirrus_payload.CirrusPayload CirrusPayload(payload).validate() is the check process runs. set_id() generates the id the same way. See CirrusPayload JSON logs carrying the payload ID in a task cirrus.lib.logging.CirrusLoggerAdapter See Structured logging Read state records or execution payloads from a script cirrus.lib.statedb.StateDB, cirrus.lib.payload_bucket.PayloadBucket Both read their configuration from CIRRUS_* environment variables, which cirrus manage <deployment> exec and call load for you. See StateDB and PayloadBucket Parse messages from the workflow event topic cirrus.lib.events.WorkflowEvent WorkflowEvent.from_message_str(body) rebuilds the event from an SNS message body. See Events Do what the CLI does, from Python cirrus.management.deployment.Deployment Deployment.from_name(name, session) resolves a deployment from Parameter Store and exposes enqueue_payload, run_workflow, get_payload_state, fetch_payload, and the rest. See Deployment class

Exceptions the library raises, and the CLI's exit-code carrying CirrusError, are on Errors and exceptions.

The reference pages that follow are generated from the source docstrings.

docs.title: Batch infrastructure
docs.text:
A Batch task is not a single CloudFormation resource. Cirrus declares no Batch resources of its own, so every Batch task supplies them: at minimum a job definition, and in practice a compute environment, a job queue, and IAM roles as well.

This page covers those resources. The state machine definition around a Batch task is in Batch tasks in a workflow.

docs.title: Declaring a Batch task
docs.text:
At minimum, a Batch task needs a job definition, a compute environment, a job queue, and the IAM resources the compute environment references. The following example declares all of them for a Reproject task:

ReprojectBatchJob:
  Type: AWS::Batch::JobDefinition
  Properties:
    JobDefinitionName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-Reproject'
    Type: Container
    Parameters:
      url: ""
      url_out: ""
    ContainerProperties:
      Command:
        - python
        - task.py
        - run
        - Ref::url
        - --output
        - Ref::url_out
      ResourceRequirements:
        - Type: VCPU
          Value: "4"
        - Type: MEMORY
          Value: "8000"
      Image: !Sub '123456789012.dkr.ecr.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/some-image-name:latest'
      JobRoleArn: !GetAtt ReprojectJobRole.Arn

ReprojectComputeEnvironment:
  Type: AWS::Batch::ComputeEnvironment
  Properties:
    Type: MANAGED
    ComputeResources:
      Type: EC2
      AllocationStrategy: BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE
      MinvCpus: 0
      MaxvCpus: 256
      SecurityGroupIds: !Ref BatchSecurityGroupIds
      Subnets: !Ref BatchSubnets
      InstanceRole: !GetAtt ReprojectInstanceProfile.Arn
    State: ENABLED

ReprojectJobQueue:
  Type: AWS::Batch::JobQueue
  Properties:
    ComputeEnvironmentOrder:
      - Order: 1
        ComputeEnvironment: !Ref ReprojectComputeEnvironment
    State: ENABLED
    Priority: 1

ReprojectInstanceRole:
  Type: AWS::IAM::Role
  Properties:
    AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
      Version: '2012-10-17'
      Statement:
        - Effect: Allow
          Principal:
            Service:
              - ec2.amazonaws.com
          Action:
            - sts:AssumeRole
    ManagedPolicyArns:
      - arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AmazonEC2ContainerServiceforEC2Role

ReprojectInstanceProfile:
  Type: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
  Properties:
    Roles:
      - Ref: ReprojectInstanceRole

ReprojectJobRole:
  Type: AWS::IAM::Role
  Properties:
    AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
      Version: '2012-10-17'
      Statement:
        - Effect: Allow
          Principal:
            Service:
              - ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com
          Action:
            - sts:AssumeRole
    Policies:
      - PolicyName: Cirrus
        PolicyDocument:
          Version: '2012-10-17'
          Statement:
            - Effect: Allow
              Action:
                - s3:GetObject
                - s3:PutObject
              Resource:
                - !Sub 'arn:aws:s3:::${CirrusPayloadBucket}/*'

The ComputeEnvironment.ServiceRole property is omitted: when left unset, AWS Batch uses its own service-linked role, which is sufficient for a standard compute environment.

docs.title: Job definition
docs.text:
The job definition is the only resource a Batch task strictly requires. It specifies the container image to run, the command to run inside it, and the container's resource requirements. See the AWS job definition CloudFormation reference for the full property list.

Job parameters. The Parameters key declares named parameters, with optional defaults, that each submission fills in. A Cirrus Batch task receives its input payload's S3 URL as url and the URL it must write its output to as url_out, both produced by pre-batch. The Command references them with the Ref:: syntax:

Command:
  - python
  - task.py
  - run
  - Ref::url
  - --output
  - Ref::url_out

which Batch expands at submission time to python task.py run <url> --output <url_out>, the stac-task command line. A task with its own entry point must read from and write to those two URLs the same way. See Batch tasks in a workflow for how the workflow passes both.

Resource requirements. ResourceRequirements sets the VCPU, MEMORY, and optionally GPU requirements for the job. These values are defaults that a submission can override through ContainerOverrides. The compute environment uses these requirements, together with its AllocationStrategy, to pick an instance type for the job.

Image. Image accepts a registry image reference (repository-url/image:tag); omitting the registry defaults to Docker Hub. Cirrus tasks typically pull from ECR. In a deployment with multiple environments, parameterizing the image tag (!Sub '...${ImageTag}', with ImageTag set per environment) lets each environment pull a distinct image version from the same repository.

docs.title: Compute environment
docs.text:
Type: MANAGED lets AWS Batch provision and scale instances; Type: EC2 compute resources give more control over instance selection than Fargate and are typically favored for compute-intensive geospatial processing.

Compute environment scaling is governed by MinvCpus, MaxvCpus, and AllocationStrategy. As jobs are submitted, the compute environment allocates instances to match the total vCPU count requested by all in-flight jobs, up to MaxvCpus, which is therefore also the practical ceiling on how many jobs can run concurrently. Setting MinvCpus above zero keeps that many vCPUs of instance capacity running at all times, which avoids cold-start latency for the first jobs of a burst at the cost of paying for idle capacity between bursts.

ComputeResources.InstanceRole takes an IAM instance profile ARN, not a role ARN. See IAM roles.

Naming compute environments

A compute environment is a replace-only resource: giving it an explicit ComputeEnvironmentName means an update that CloudFormation cannot perform in place (for example, changing ComputeResources.Type) fails on a name conflict between the existing environment and its replacement, rather than replacing it automatically. Omitting the name avoids that failure mode but produces autogenerated names. See Updating Batch resources safely for the tradeoffs this creates during updates.

docs.title: Job queue
docs.text: A job is submitted to a job queue, not directly to a compute environment. The queue holds submitted jobs when the compute environment is saturated, and ComputeEnvironmentOrder can list more than one compute environment per queue, for example to prefer an On-Demand environment and overflow into a Spot environment. See the AWS job queue CloudFormation reference for supported configuration, including scheduling policies for prioritizing jobs within a shared queue.

docs.title: IAM roles
docs.text:
A compute environment references two IAM identities:

  • ServiceRole is used by AWS Batch itself. Omit this property to use the AWS-managed service-linked role; a custom role is only needed for non-standard Batch permissions.
  • ComputeResources.InstanceRole is the role for each EC2 container instance, supplied as an instance profile ARN rather than a role ARN. The instance role needs at minimum the AmazonEC2ContainerServiceforEC2Role managed policy so the ECS agent can register the instance and pull images; the example above pairs an AWS::IAM::Role with an AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile that references it.

A separate role, the job definition's ContainerProperties.JobRoleArn, is assumed by the running container itself and should carry the permissions the task's code needs (for example, S3 read/write on the payload bucket). Keeping the instance role and the job role separate means the ECS agent's permissions and the task code's permissions don't have to match, and a compute environment shared by multiple job definitions doesn't grant every task the union of all their permissions.

docs.title: Using the AWS Spot market
docs.text:
Spot instances reduce cost relative to On-Demand, at the cost of instances being reclaimed by AWS with little notice. A compute environment opts into Spot with Type: SPOT:

ComputeResources:
  Type: SPOT
  AllocationStrategy: BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE
  SpotIamFleetRole: !GetAtt EC2SpotRole.Arn
  InstanceRole: !GetAtt BatchInstanceProfile.Arn
  InstanceTypes:
    - r5.xlarge
    - r5.2xlarge
    - r5.4xlarge
  MinvCpus: 0
  MaxvCpus: 5000

SpotIamFleetRole is required only when AllocationStrategy is BEST_FIT or unset; the progressive and capacity-optimized strategies do not use it. BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE requests progressively across the listed instance types that best match the job's resource requirements, accepting any of them, which tends to fill Spot capacity faster than BEST_FIT (which waits for its single best-fit type). Restricting InstanceTypes to a set with a consistent vCPU-to-memory ratio matching the job's ResourceRequirements avoids wasting the unused capacity of an oversized instance.

Because Spot reclamation surfaces as a killed job, error handling in the workflow matters more with Spot than with On-Demand. See Batch retries vs. Step Functions retries.

docs.title: Launch templates
docs.text:
A launch template customizes the EC2 instances a compute environment starts, most commonly to increase the root EBS volume size beyond its default, since a Batch job's ResourceRequirements cannot request disk space directly:

ReprojectLaunchTemplate:
  Type: AWS::EC2::LaunchTemplate
  Properties:
    LaunchTemplateData:
      BlockDeviceMappings:
        - DeviceName: /dev/xvda
          Ebs:
            VolumeSize: 500
            VolumeType: gp3
            DeleteOnTermination: true
            Encrypted: true

referenced from the compute environment as:

LaunchTemplate:
  LaunchTemplateId: !Ref ReprojectLaunchTemplate
  Version: $Latest

Updating a launch template does not affect any compute environment already running against it: the launch template version is resolved once, at compute environment creation, and cached. Making a launch template change take effect on an existing compute environment requires recreating the compute environment so it re-resolves $Latest (or whichever version is referenced). See Updating Batch resources safely.

docs.title: Other considerations
docs.text:
Shared resources. Prefer a dedicated job definition, compute environment, and job queue per Batch task over sharing them across tasks. Sharing reduces duplication but couples the tasks' resource requirements, instance selection, and IAM permissions together, and increases the blast radius of any single resource change.

Batch quotas. AWS limits an account to 50 compute environments and 50 job queues per Region. A deployment with many Batch tasks, especially one using the blue/green update strategy below, which doubles the resource count per task while a change is rolling out, needs enough quota headroom for that doubling, or needs to consolidate compute environments and job queues across tasks.

Subnets. Compute resources in a private subnet incur NAT Gateway data processing charges for traffic leaving the VPC (for example, pulling images from ECR or reading/writing S3 in another Region). Where the security posture allows it, a public subnet avoids that cost. Restrict inbound access with security groups regardless. In particular, do not open SSH (port 22) to compute instances.

docs.title: Batch tasks in a workflow
docs.text:
Step Functions passes a Lambda task its input directly. AWS Batch has no equivalent channel: a SubmitJob request carries only small string parameters, not a Cirrus Payload. Cirrus bridges the gap with two core Lambda functions, pre-batch and post-batch, that the workflow runs immediately before and after each Batch task.

This page covers the state machine definition around a Batch task. The CloudFormation for the task itself, meaning the job definition, compute environment, job queue, and IAM, is in Batch infrastructure.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
pre-batch uploads the state input to S3 and returns {"url": ..., "url_out": ...}. The Batch job reads its input payload from url and writes its output payload to url_out. post-batch reads url_out and returns the payload to the state machine, so the next state receives a Cirrus Payload as it would from a Lambda task. The workflow's job is to pass url and url_out from pre-batch's output into the Batch task's Parameters, and to route a failed job's error into post-batch so it can surface the job's own exception. See Lambda functions for what each function does with failures.

The three steps and the bucket they pass the payload through, alongside an ordinary Lambda task for comparison:

flowchart LR
    subgraph sm["State machine"]
        direction LR
        L["Lambda task"] --> PB
        subgraph par["Parallel block"]
            direction LR
            PB["pre-batch\nLambda function"] --> J["Batch job"] --> QB["post-batch\nLambda function"]
        end
    end
    PB -- "writes payload to url" --> B[("Payload bucket")]
    B -- "reads url" --> J
    J -- "writes url_out" --> B
    B -- "reads url_out" --> QB
    J -. "assets" .-> D[("Data bucket")]

docs.title: Group the three steps in a Parallel block
docs.text:
A Batch task in a workflow is really three Step Functions steps: pre-batch, the Batch task, and post-batch. Because they only make sense together, they should share error handling and retries: if any one of the three fails in a way that isn't retried, the whole group should fail.

Step Functions' Parallel state supports Retry and Catch like a Task state, and accepts one or more branches. Using Parallel with a single branch groups the three steps into one unit from the perspective of retries and failure, without actually running anything concurrently.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Failures are more varied with Batch than with Lambda. A SubmitJob call can fail with Batch.AWSBatchException when too many jobs are submitted too quickly. A running job can be killed and need to be retried when its underlying EC2 instance is reclaimed, which happens routinely with Spot instances at scale. Wrapping the Batch task step in a Parallel block with a Retry policy handles both cases without retrying pre-batch or post-batch unnecessarily.

The Parallel block's own Catch must route to a Fail state that uses ErrorPath/CausePath (not static Error/Cause) so the error captured from a failed Batch job or Lambda function is preserved rather than replaced with a fixed string. See Workflows: Capturing errors for why this matters and how update-state consumes it.

For retry IntervalSeconds/BackoffRate/MaxAttempts/JitterStrategy semantics, see Workflows: Retry with backoff and jitter.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The definition below is written as the body of a CloudFormation !Sub, so ${ExampleJobQueue} and ${ExampleBatchJob} resolve to the job queue and job definition resources in the same template.

{
    "Comment": "Example workflow using Parallel to group a Batch task with pre-batch/post-batch",
    "StartAt": "batch-group",
    "States": {
        "batch-group": {
            "Type": "Parallel",
            "Branches": [
                {
                    "StartAt": "pre-batch",
                    "States": {
                        "pre-batch": {
                            "Type": "Task",
                            "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
                            "Parameters": {
                                "FunctionName": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:my-prefix-pre-batch",
                                "Payload.$": "$"
                            },
                            "OutputPath": "$.Payload",
                            "Next": "batch-task",
                            "Retry": [
                                {
                                    "ErrorEquals": [
                                        "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException",
                                        "Lambda.Unknown"
                                    ],
                                    "IntervalSeconds": 10,
                                    "MaxDelaySeconds": 86400,
                                    "BackoffRate": 2,
                                    "MaxAttempts": 20,
                                    "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
                                }
                            ]
                        },
                        "batch-task": {
                            "Type": "Task",
                            "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::batch:submitJob.sync",
                            "Parameters": {
                                "JobName": "some-batch-job",
                                "JobQueue": "${ExampleJobQueue}",
                                "JobDefinition": "${ExampleBatchJob}",
                                "Parameters": {
                                    "url.$": "$.url",
                                    "url_out.$": "$.url_out"
                                }
                            },
                            "Next": "post-batch",
                            "Retry": [
                                {
                                    "ErrorEquals": [
                                        "Batch.AWSBatchException"
                                    ],
                                    "IntervalSeconds": 600,
                                    "MaxDelaySeconds": 86400,
                                    "BackoffRate": 2,
                                    "MaxAttempts": 20,
                                    "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
                                }
                            ],
                            "Catch": [
                                {
                                    "ErrorEquals": [
                                        "States.ALL"
                                    ],
                                    "ResultPath": "$.error",
                                    "Next": "post-batch"
                                }
                            ]
                        },
                        "post-batch": {
                            "Type": "Task",
                            "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
                            "Parameters": {
                                "FunctionName": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:my-prefix-post-batch",
                                "Payload.$": "$"
                            },
                            "OutputPath": "$.Payload",
                            "End": true,
                            "Retry": [
                                {
                                    "ErrorEquals": [
                                        "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException",
                                        "Lambda.Unknown"
                                    ],
                                    "IntervalSeconds": 10,
                                    "MaxDelaySeconds": 86400,
                                    "BackoffRate": 2,
                                    "MaxAttempts": 20,
                                    "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
                                }
                            ]
                        }
                    }
                }
            ],
            "Next": "publish",
            "OutputPath": "$[0]",
            "Retry": [
                {
                    "ErrorEquals": [
                        "States.ALL"
                    ],
                    "MaxAttempts": 3,
                    "IntervalSeconds": 1200,
                    "MaxDelaySeconds": 86400,
                    "BackoffRate": 2,
                    "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
                }
            ],
            "Catch": [
                {
                    "ErrorEquals": [
                        "States.ALL"
                    ],
                    "ResultPath": "$.error",
                    "Next": "failure"
                }
            ]
        },
        "publish": {
            "Type": "Task",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
            "Parameters": {
                "FunctionName": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:my-prefix-publish",
                "Payload.$": "$"
            },
            "End": true,
            "Retry": [
                {
                    "ErrorEquals": [
                        "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException",
                        "Lambda.Unknown"
                    ],
                    "IntervalSeconds": 10,
                    "MaxDelaySeconds": 86400,
                    "BackoffRate": 2,
                    "MaxAttempts": 20,
                    "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
                }
            ],
            "Catch": [
                {
                    "ErrorEquals": [
                        "States.ALL"
                    ],
                    "ResultPath": "$.error",
                    "Next": "failure"
                }
            ]
        },
        "failure": {
            "Type": "Fail",
            "ErrorPath": "$.error.Error",
            "CausePath": "$.error.Cause"
        }
    }
}

The Batch task step catches its own errors (Catch routing to post-batch on States.ALL) so that post-batch always runs, even after a Batch job failure, and can turn the raw Batch failure into the underlying container error before it propagates further. The outer Parallel block then retries or fails the whole pre-batch/Batch/post-batch group as a unit.

docs.title: Batch retries vs. Step Functions retries
docs.text: Prefer Step Functions' Retry (as above) over relying on AWS Batch's own job retry configuration. Batch retries apply uniformly regardless of failure reason, while Step Functions Retry blocks match specific error types, giving more control over what gets retried versus failed outright. Step Functions retries also appear as distinct steps in the execution history, making a retried attempt and its original failure visible to anyone investigating the run; Batch's own retries are internal to the job and are not reflected in the state machine execution.

docs.title: Batch errors and InvalidInput
docs.text: A Batch task that finds its input unprocessable should raise stactask.exceptions.InvalidInput like a Lambda task would. post-batch reads the job's last log line, which for an uncaught Python exception is stactask.exceptions.InvalidInput: <message>, and re-raises it under that name, so update-state records the execution as INVALID rather than FAILED. See Raising InvalidInput.

docs.title: Chaining workflows
docs.text:
Chaining runs workflow executions in sequence, with the output payload of one becoming the input payload of the next. It is expressed in the payload itself: the process array holds one process definition per link, and each execution consumes the first entry. A payload chaining two workflows:

{
    "process": [
        { "workflow": "workflow-1" },
        { "workflow": "workflow-2" }
    ]
}

flowchart LR
  1(Workflow 1)
  2(Workflow 2)
  1 --> 2

An entry after the first can itself be an array, which fans out: one execution per element, each continuing independently with the rest of the chain.

{
    "process": [
        { "workflow": "workflow-1" },
        [
            { "workflow": "workflow-2a" },
            { "workflow": "workflow-2b" }
        ],
        { "workflow": "workflow-3" }
    ]
}

flowchart LR
  1(Workflow 1)
  2a(Workflow 2a)
  2b(Workflow 2b)
  3a(Workflow 3)
  3b(Workflow 3)
  1 --> 2a
  1 --> 2b
  2a --> 3a
  2b --> 3b

Chaining expresses one-to-one and one-to-many dependencies. It has no way to merge branches back together, and a branch element cannot itself contain a nested array.

docs.title: How chaining runs
docs.text:
When an execution reaches SUCCEEDED, the update-state function calls PayloadManager.next_payloads on the execution's output payload and, when CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL is set, sends each result to the process queue. From there it is an ordinary incoming payload: process picks it up and starts the next execution.

flowchart LR
  sfn1[Workflow 1 execution]
  us[update-state]
  q[Process queue]
  proc[process]
  sfn2[Workflow 2 execution]
  sfn1 -- terminal event --> us
  us -- next payload --> q
  q --> proc
  proc -- starts execution --> sfn2

next_payloads (cirrus.lib.payload_manager) builds each next payload from a deep copy of the output payload:

  • The first process entry, the definition just run, is removed.
  • If nothing remains, the chain ends and nothing is enqueued.
  • If the next entry is a single definition, one payload is produced with it as process[0]. If it is an array, one payload is produced per element.
  • The id is deleted. process generates a new one from the output items and the next workflow name, so a chained execution never reuses the previous execution's ID.
  • If the next definition has a chain_filter, features is reduced to the items that match it.

Only SUCCEEDED executions chain. A FAILED, INVALID, ABORTED, or timed-out execution enqueues nothing, and a succeeded execution with no output payload enqueues nothing either.

docs.title: Filtering output items
docs.text:
When the next workflow needs only some of the preceding workflow's output items, set chain_filter on its process definition to a JSONPath filter expression. To keep only items whose id starts with SWE and whose confidence property exceeds 80:

{
    "process": [
        { "workflow": "workflow-1" },
        {
            "workflow": "workflow-2",
            "chain_filter": "@.id =~ 'SWE.*' & @.properties.confidence > 80"
        }
    ]
}

The expression is substituted into $.features[?(<chain_filter>)] and evaluated with jsonpath-ng against the output payload, so the example evaluates:

$.features[?(@.id =~ 'SWE.*' & @.properties.confidence > 80)]

Only the matching items are carried into the next payload's features. A filter that matches nothing produces a payload with an empty features array, which process rejects because it cannot generate an id without items.

docs.title: Feeders
docs.text: A feeder is whatever puts a Cirrus Payload on the process queue. Cirrus ships none: src/ has no feeder base class or CLI subcommand, and cloudformation/ provisions no feeder resources. Discovering new data, choosing a workflow, and building the payload are the deployment's own code, run on its own compute. That can be a Lambda function behind an S3 event notification, a scheduled job that polls an external API, or a person running cirrus manage <deployment> process from a shell.

docs.title: What the queue accepts
docs.text:
The process function is the queue's only consumer. Its extract_record step accepts a message body that is any of:

  • a Cirrus Payload, as JSON;
  • a reference of the form {"url": "s3://bucket/key"} to a payload object, which process fetches. Its role can read any bucket, so the object does not have to be in the payload bucket;
  • an SNS delivery envelope whose Message field holds either of the above, which is what SNS delivers when the queue is subscribed to a topic without raw message delivery.

The payload must pass CirrusPayload.validate: a process array with at least one entry, a workflow name in the first entry, and, if present, an id in the <collections>/workflow-<workflow>/<itemids> form. A missing id is generated from the items and workflow name; see ID format. A message that cannot be parsed or fails validation is uploaded to the payload bucket's invalid prefix and, after five receives, moved to the dead-letter queue. See Monitoring: Dead-letter queues.

SQS accepts messages up to 256 KB. A larger payload must be stored in S3 and sent as a {"url": ...} reference. The Cirrus CLI does this itself, uploading to the payload bucket's oversized prefix, and a Python feeder can do the same with PayloadBucket.upload_oversize_payload from cirrus.lib.payload_bucket.

docs.title: Sending to the queue
docs.text:
The queue is ${ResourcePrefix}-process. Its URL is the ProcessQueueUrl output of the main stack and the CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL entry under the deployment's Parameter Store prefix. The feeder's identity needs sqs:SendMessage on the queue.

A feeder can also publish to an SNS topic that the queue is subscribed to, which suits a trigger that already arrives as an SNS notification. No such topic exists in this repository's templates. The two topics the base stack creates, ${ResourcePrefix}-publish and ${ResourcePrefix}-workflow-event, are outputs, not inputs. The following is one way to add one, in the style of the templates in cloudformation/core/:

# Illustrative. Not part of the in-repo templates. ProcessQueueArn and
# ProcessQueueUrl are the base stack outputs of the same names.
Resources:
  NewDataTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      TopicName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-new-data'

  NewDataToProcessQueue:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Subscription
    Properties:
      TopicArn: !Ref NewDataTopic
      Protocol: sqs
      Endpoint: !Ref ProcessQueueArn
      RawMessageDelivery: false

  ProcessQueuePolicy:
    Type: AWS::SQS::QueuePolicy
    Properties:
      Queues:
        - !Ref ProcessQueueUrl
      PolicyDocument:
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: sns.amazonaws.com
            Action: sqs:SendMessage
            Resource: !Ref ProcessQueueArn
            Condition:
              ArnEquals:
                aws:SourceArn: !Ref NewDataTopic

With RawMessageDelivery: false, SNS wraps the published message in its envelope and process unwraps it, so the feeder publishes the payload JSON as the message body unchanged.

docs.title: A minimal Python feeder
docs.text:
A Lambda handler that takes one STAC item, builds a payload for a workflow named my-workflow, and sends it directly to the queue:

import json
import os

import boto3

sqs = boto3.client("sqs")

QUEUE_URL = os.environ["CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL"]


def build_payload(item: dict) -> dict:
    collection = item["collection"]
    item_id = item["id"]
    workflow = "my-workflow"

    return {
        "type": "FeatureCollection",
        "id": f"{collection}/workflow-{workflow}/{item_id}",
        "features": [item],
        "process": [
            {
                "workflow": workflow,
                "upload_options": {
                    "path_template": "s3://my-data-bucket/${collection}/${id}",
                },
            },
        ],
    }


def lambda_handler(event, context):
    item = event["item"]
    payload = build_payload(item)

    sqs.send_message(
        QueueUrl=QUEUE_URL,
        MessageBody=json.dumps(payload),
    )

    return payload["id"]

The id is set explicitly because it is one collection and one item. A feeder that submits several items per payload can omit id and let process derive it, which sorts and joins the collections and item IDs deterministically. A feeder that wants to catch a malformed payload before sending it can call CirrusPayload(payload).validate() from cirrus.lib.cirrus_payload, which is the same check process runs.

docs.title: Writing a task
docs.text: A task is one processing step in a workflow. It takes a Cirrus Payload in and returns one, modifying the items and writing any assets it produces to S3 on the way. Tasks are the code a pipeline is mostly made of. Cirrus does not define a task interface beyond the payload contract, so a task is any Lambda function or Batch job the workflow's state machine can invoke.

docs.title: What a task does
docs.text:
1. Receive a Cirrus Payload. For a Lambda task this is the state input. For a Batch task it is the S3 URL in the url job parameter.
  2. Read the parameters meant for it from the process definition.
  3. Download whatever assets it needs from the items in features.
  4. Do the processing: derive new assets, compute new metadata, or transform metadata into STAC.
  5. Upload output assets to S3 and update the items' asset hrefs to point at them.
  6. Return the payload with features replaced by the output items. A Lambda task returns it as its response. A Batch task writes it to the URL in the url_out job parameter.

stac-task, a dependency of Cirrus, provides a Task base class that handles everything but step 4. Subclass it, set a name class attribute, and implement process, which receives the task's parameters as keyword arguments and returns the output items as dicts:

from typing import Any

from stactask import Task


class MyTask(Task):
    name = "my-task"
    description = "One sentence for --help"

    def process(self, **kwargs: Any) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        items = self.items_as_dicts
        ...
        return items


handler = MyTask.handler

Task.handler is the Lambda entry point. It reads a {"url": ...} input by fetching that object, which is how an oversized payload arrives, and after process returns it applies the process definition's collection_matchers to the output items and returns the payload. Task.cli is the Batch entry point: python task.py run <input-url> --output <output-url> reads the input from the first URL and writes the output payload to the second. The handler does not write an oversized output back to S3; a Lambda task whose output could exceed the size limit should be a Batch task instead.

docs.title: Task parameters
docs.text: A task reads its parameters from Task.parameters, which merges the process definition's workflow_options with the task's own entry under tasks, keyed by the task's name, with the task's entry winning on conflicts. Both are described under Process definition.

docs.title: Lambda or Batch
docs.text:
A task runs as a Lambda function or an AWS Batch job. Both can be built from one container image; the choice is about runtime limits.

Lambda suits a task that finishes within the 15-minute maximum timeout and fits in 10 GB of memory and 10 GB of ephemeral storage. Lambda sets CPU in proportion to memory, so a task cannot choose its core count. Batch suits a task that runs longer, needs more memory or storage, a specific vCPU-to-memory ratio, or a GPU. A Batch task also needs its own CloudFormation resources and the pre-batch and post-batch states around it in the workflow, so Lambda is the lower-overhead default.

docs.title: When Batch overhead dominates
docs.text:
Submitting a Batch job carries a fixed cost, since placing the job on an instance can take minutes, regardless of how long the job itself runs. When a task's real work is short, that overhead dominates its runtime and cost, and it should be a Lambda task. Two cases from Earth Search:

  • Landsat ingest reads the public-c2-notify-v2 SNS topic, which includes many Real-Time scenes that are filtered out after seconds of work. Running that filter as a Batch job would spend minutes of placement, and the corresponding EC2 cost, on each. Landsat ingest as a whole is a metadata-to-metadata conversion taking tens of seconds per scene, so it runs entirely on Lambda.
  • The Sentinel-2 Collection 1 Level-2A collection includes only items with processing baseline 05.00 or higher. During a full back-processing run, roughly half the scenes had an older baseline and were discarded immediately, while the rest ran a five-to-ten-minute Batch job. The discarded half still paid the placement overhead. A Lambda step checking the baseline ahead of the Batch job would have avoided it.

docs.title: Container image
docs.text:
Package a task as a container image unless it will only ever run on Lambda and has few dependencies, which is rare for geospatial processing. Lambda and Batch need different ENTRYPOINT and CMD settings, so build one base image with everything else and derive two thin images from it.

A base image built on the AWS Lambda Python image already has ENTRYPOINT ["/lambda-entrypoint.sh"], the runtime interface client that Lambda requires. The example below adds GDAL from a prebuilt layer image and the task's dependencies:

FROM ghcr.io/lambgeo/lambda-gdal:3.8-python3.11 AS gdal

FROM public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.11

COPY --from=gdal /opt/lib/ ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/lib/
COPY --from=gdal /opt/include/ ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/include/
COPY --from=gdal /opt/share/ ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/share/
COPY --from=gdal /opt/bin/ ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/bin/

ENV \
  GDAL_DATA=${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/share/gdal \
  PROJ_LIB=${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/share/proj \
  GDAL_CONFIG=${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/bin/gdal-config \
  GEOS_CONFIG=${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/bin/geos-config \
  PATH=${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/bin:$PATH

COPY requirements.txt ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}
RUN pip3 install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY src/task/task.py ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}/task.py

The Lambda image keeps the inherited entrypoint and names the handler:

FROM my-base-task

CMD [ "task.handler" ]

The Batch image clears the entrypoint so the job definition's Command runs directly:

FROM my-base-task

ENTRYPOINT []

Clearing ENTRYPOINT also resets any inherited CMD. The job definition supplies the command, for example python task.py run Ref::url --output Ref::url_out; see Batch infrastructure: Job definition. A base image that is not derived from an AWS Lambda image must add the Lambda runtime interface client itself for the Lambda variant to work.

docs.title: Structured logging
docs.text:
cirrus.lib.logging configures Python's logging module at import time. Loggers named task, feeder, function, lambda_function, cirrus.lib, and their children, get JSON output through pythonjsonlogger at the level in CIRRUS_LOG_LEVEL, default DEBUG. A task gets structured logging by naming its logger under one of those prefixes.

CirrusLoggerAdapter wraps such a logger and attaches the payload's id and stac_version to every record when constructed with the payload, plus aws_request_id when given one:

from cirrus.lib.logging import CirrusLoggerAdapter

logger = CirrusLoggerAdapter("task.my-task", payload=payload)

logger.info("processing %d items", len(payload["features"]))

The adapter also stops the parent logger from propagating to the root logger, which prevents each line appearing twice in CloudWatch under Lambda's own root handler. Filtering a log group by payload ID is then a search for that ID string; see Isolating one Lambda invocation.

A task built on stac-task gets a logger named after its name attribute through the base class. That logger is not under a Cirrus prefix, so to get Cirrus's JSON format a stac-task task should name itself task.<something> or wrap logging.getLogger("task." + self.name) itself.

docs.title: Raising InvalidInput
docs.text:
When a task determines that its input can never be processed, as opposed to failing for a transient reason, it should raise stactask.exceptions.InvalidInput. update-state recognizes that error name and records the execution as INVALID instead of FAILED, and process will not rerun an INVALID payload unless the process definition sets replace. Any other exception records FAILED, which reruns on resubmission. See Lambda functions: Status to state.

For a Batch task the same rule holds. post-batch reads the job's last log line and re-raises the exception under the name it finds there, so an uncaught InvalidInput in the container still reaches update-state by name.

docs.title: Defining a workflow
docs.text:
A workflow is an AWS Step Functions state machine, written in Amazon States Language, that runs a payload through a sequence of tasks. Cirrus starts an execution of it per payload and records the outcome. Everything between start and finish is the state machine's own definition.

A workflow deploys as its own CloudFormation stack containing an AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine and the IAM role it assumes to invoke its tasks. The in-repo minimal workflow (cloudformation/workflows/minimal/state_machine.yaml) is the smallest complete example: one Choice state that succeeds or fails on a field in the payload, with no tasks at all.

AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: 'Cirrus - Minimal Workflow Step Function'

Parameters:
  ResourcePrefix:
    Type: String
    Description: Prefix for all resource names

Resources:
  MinimalWorkflowStateMachine:
    Type: AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine
    Properties:
      StateMachineName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-minimal'
      RoleArn: !GetAtt StateMachineRole.Arn
      DefinitionString: |
        {
          "Comment": "Minimal workflow for testing",
          "StartAt": "CheckWorkflow",
          "States": {
            "CheckWorkflow": {
              "Type": "Choice",
              "Choices": [
                {
                  "Variable": "$.process[0].succeed",
                  "BooleanEquals": true,
                  "Next": "Success"
                }
              ],
              "Default": "FailState"
            },
            "Success": {
              "Type": "Succeed"
            },
            "FailState": {
              "Type": "Fail",
              "Error": "WorkflowMismatch",
              "Cause": "The succeed field was not true"
            }
          }
        }

  StateMachineRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-minimal-workflow-role'
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: states.amazonaws.com
            Action: 'sts:AssumeRole'
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - 'arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/CloudWatchLogsFullAccess'

Because minimal has no tasks, its Fail state can use static Error and Cause strings. A workflow with tasks should capture the failing task's error instead. See Capturing errors.

docs.title: Naming and dispatch
docs.text:
The state machine must be named ${ResourcePrefix}-<workflow>, where <workflow> is the name a payload's process definition uses in its workflow field. This convention is the only link between the core stack and a workflow stack:

  • The process function builds the state machine ARN by appending the workflow name to CIRRUS_BASE_WORKFLOW_ARN, which cloudformation/core/functions.yaml sets to arn:aws:states:<region>:<account>:stateMachine:${ResourcePrefix}-. Its IAM role allows states:StartExecution only on ARNs with that prefix.
  • The EventBridge rule that invokes update-state matches stateMachineArn against the same prefix, so a state machine outside the convention finishes without its outcome being recorded.

Workflow names must not contain underscores. The state database joins the collections and workflow name with an underscore and splits on the last one to recover them. See ID format.

docs.title: State machine structure
docs.text:
Every workflow definition has:

  • StartAt naming the first state.
  • At least one state that ends the execution successfully: End: true on a Task state, or a Succeed state.
  • A Fail state that each task's Catch routes to, so that a task error ends the execution as FAILED with the error preserved.

A task that invokes a Lambda function uses the arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke resource with the function ARN in Parameters.FunctionName, rather than naming the function ARN as the state's Resource. This integration records the Lambda request ID in the execution history, which is what get-execution-events --with-log-metadata uses to find the invocation's logs. It also wraps the function's return value in a Payload field, so the state needs "OutputPath": "$.Payload" to pass the Cirrus Payload itself, and not the invoke response, to the next state or to the execution output.

{
    "Comment": "Example workflow with a single Lambda task",
    "StartAt": "my-task",
    "States": {
        "my-task": {
            "Type": "Task",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
            "Parameters": {
                "FunctionName": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:my-prefix-my-task",
                "Payload.$": "$"
            },
            "OutputPath": "$.Payload",
            "End": true,
            "Retry": [
                {
                    "ErrorEquals": [
                        "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException",
                        "Lambda.Unknown"
                    ],
                    "IntervalSeconds": 1,
                    "BackoffRate": 2,
                    "MaxAttempts": 5
                }
            ],
            "Catch": [
                {
                    "ErrorEquals": [
                        "States.ALL"
                    ],
                    "ResultPath": "$.error",
                    "Next": "failure"
                }
            ]
        },
        "failure": {
            "Type": "Fail",
            "ErrorPath": "$.error.Error",
            "CausePath": "$.error.Cause"
        }
    }
}

"Payload.$": "$" passes the whole state input, the Cirrus Payload, to the function. update-state parses the execution's final output as a Cirrus Payload, so the last state's output must be the payload, not a wrapper around it.

A workflow mixes Lambda and Batch tasks freely; Batch is a property of a task, not of the workflow. A Batch task needs pre-batch and post-batch states around it and a different retry structure. See Batch tasks in a workflow.

docs.title: Retry with backoff and jitter
docs.text:
Some errors occur before a task runs: Lambda.TooManyRequestsException when the account's Lambda concurrency is exhausted, or Batch.AWSBatchException when the SubmitJob rate limit is hit. Retrying immediately tends to fail again for the same reason, so each task's Retry should back off:

{
    "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.Unknown"],
    "IntervalSeconds": 600,
    "MaxDelaySeconds": 86400,
    "BackoffRate": 2.0,
    "MaxAttempts": 20,
    "JitterStrategy": "FULL"
}

IntervalSeconds is the first delay. Each later delay is the previous one multiplied by BackoffRate, capped at MaxDelaySeconds, for up to MaxAttempts attempts. JitterStrategy: FULL draws each delay at random between zero and the computed value, so many executions that failed together do not retry together. The default, NONE, waits the full computed delay every time.

docs.title: Capturing errors
docs.text:
update-state records a failed execution's error from the error and cause fields of the EventBridge status-change event. Step Functions fills those from the Fail state that ended the execution. For the task's own error to reach the state database, the task's Catch must store it in the state and the Fail state must read it back with ErrorPath and CausePath:

"Catch": [
  {
    "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"],
    "ResultPath": "$.error",
    "Next": "failure"
  }
]

"failure": {
    "Type": "Fail",
    "ErrorPath": "$.error.Error",
    "CausePath": "$.error.Cause"
}

A Fail state with static Error and Cause strings records those strings instead of the task's error. A Fail state with none of these fields leaves cause empty, and update-state stores a fixed message telling the reader to add ErrorPath and CausePath. The error name also decides whether the execution is recorded FAILED or INVALID. See Lambda functions: Status to state.

docs.title: Triggering workflows off one another
docs.text:
Two ways to model a pipeline as connected workflows:

  • Chaining. A payload's process array lists several process definitions, and the output of each execution becomes the input of the next. See Chaining workflows.
  • Publish topic subscriptions. Any subscriber to the publish SNS topic receives each output item as update-state publishes it, and can build and enqueue a new payload from it. This decouples the downstream workflow from the payload that produced the item.

docs.title: Design guidance
docs.text:
Cirrus enforces none of the following. They keep a deployment easier to reason about.

One input item per workflow. State is tracked per payload ID, and the ID is derived from the input item IDs, so a workflow that takes one item has one record per item and a plain rerun story. Where several inputs are unavoidable, a synthetic item that resolves to the real inputs deterministically keeps the single-item interface.

Short workflows. A workflow should model one level of processing. Needing to persist intermediate outputs partway through is a sign it should be two workflows chained together.

Same inputs, same outputs. Cirrus decides whether to run a payload from its ID, which encodes only the workflow name, collections, and item IDs. Process definition parameters are not part of that decision, so two submissions that differ only in parameters are the same payload to Cirrus and the second is skipped. Do not rely on parameters to change what a workflow produces.

Specific over flexible. Parameters that select between behaviors make executions of the same workflow incomparable and conflict with the rule above. Restrict runtime parameters to values that do not change the type or content of the output items.

No side-effect workflows. A workflow transforms an input payload into output items. A workflow whose purpose is a side effect for every payload it sees belongs outside Cirrus, as a subscriber to the publish or workflow event topic.

Small payloads. Payloads travel inline through SQS, Step Functions, and EventBridge. Above 120,000 escaped bytes they are swapped for an S3 reference, which adds a round trip to every step, and an output above EventBridge's limit is dropped from the terminal event and never recorded. See Payload bucket: Oversized payloads.

AWS's best practices for Step Functions cover the rest.

docs.title: Common workflows
docs.text:
Worked examples composing cirrus commands for routine operations. Every command's options are in the Command reference. The examples use a deployment named name-dev; substitute a name from cirrus list-deployments.

Commands that take a payload read it from standard input, so a payload comes in from a file with <payload.json and pipes from one command to the next.

docs.title: Run a workflow and wait for the result
docs.text:
<payload.json cirrus manage name-dev run-workflow

run-workflow validates the payload, enqueues it, and polls the state database every 15 seconds until the record leaves PROCESSING. Then it prints the output payload and exits with a code that scripts and smoke tests can check:

Exit code Meaning 0 SUCCEEDED; the output payload is printed 10 Any other terminal state; the record's last_error is printed 11 Still PROCESSING after --timeout seconds, default 3600

--poll-interval changes the polling period. The polling starts from the record's current state, so a payload whose record is already terminal from an earlier run, resubmitted with replace, returns that earlier outcome at once rather than waiting for the rerun. Use process and then get-state for reruns.

To enqueue without waiting:

<payload.json cirrus manage name-dev process

The two differ in where a bad payload is caught. run-workflow runs CirrusPayload.validate locally before submitting, so a payload missing process, missing a workflow name, or with a malformed id fails in the shell. It also requires the payload to have an id. process submits the payload as is, and validation happens in the process Lambda function, which sends a rejected payload to the payload bucket's invalid prefix without creating a state database record. The only trace is a workflow event and, after retries, a message on the dead-letter queue.

Both commands upload a payload larger than the SQS message limit to the payload bucket and enqueue a reference to it, so large payloads need no special handling.

docs.title: Inspect an execution
docs.text:
The execution commands take --payload-id, which resolves to the payload's most recent execution, or --arn:

cirrus manage name-dev get-execution --payload-id sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1
cirrus manage name-dev get-execution --arn arn:aws:states:us-west-2:123456789012:execution:name-dev-publish:<execution-id>

From summary to event history to task logs:

cirrus manage name-dev get-execution-input --payload-id sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1
cirrus manage name-dev get-execution-output --payload-id sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1

# event history, with log group and request ID added to Lambda and Batch
# task events
cirrus manage name-dev get-execution-events --payload-id sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1 --with-log-metadata

# the logs those events point at
cirrus manage name-dev get-lambda-logs /aws/lambda/name-dev-my-task <request-id>
cirrus manage name-dev get-batch-logs <log-stream-name>

Both log commands print 20 events by default and a Next page token line when there are more, to pass back as --next-token. get-batch-logs reads from /aws/batch/job unless --log-group says otherwise.

The state machine definition behind a workflow:

cirrus manage name-dev get-workflow-definition publish

docs.title: Check state and stored payloads
docs.text:
# the state database record, as stored
cirrus manage name-dev get-state sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1

# the input and output payloads of the most recent execution
cirrus manage name-dev get-input-payload sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1
cirrus manage name-dev get-output-payload sentinel2/workflow-publish/S2A_1

get-state retries with backoff for up to 60 seconds when the record does not exist yet, so it can be called immediately after process. get-output-payload fails for any record not in SUCCEEDED, since only a succeeded execution writes an output payload.

docs.title: Query the state database in bulk
docs.text:
query prints matching records, one JSON object per line. --collections-workflow is required, in the <collections>_<workflow> form of the table's partition key. --state, --since, --limit (at most 50,000), and --error-prefix narrow the result:

cirrus manage name-dev query --collections-workflow sentinel2_publish --state FAILED --since 1d

--since is an integer followed by d, h, or m. --error-prefix matches the start of last_error, which begins with the error type, so --error-prefix stactask.exceptions.InvalidInput selects one class of failure.

get-input-payloads takes the same filters and prints each matching record's input payload instead of the record:

cirrus manage name-dev get-input-payloads --collections-workflow sentinel2_publish --state FAILED --since 10d

docs.title: Rerun failed workflows in bulk
docs.text:
get-input-payloads --rerun sets replace: true on each payload's first process definition before printing it, so process will run it again even from a state it would otherwise skip. process takes one payload per invocation, so feed the lines through one at a time:

cirrus manage name-dev get-input-payloads \
    --collections-workflow sentinel2_publish --state FAILED --since 10d --rerun |
while IFS= read -r payload; do
    printf '%s' "$payload" | cirrus manage name-dev process
done

Which states rerun without replace and which need it is defined in The replace field and reruns.

docs.title: Invoke a Lambda function directly
docs.text:
invoke-lambda calls one of the deployment's functions synchronously with an event from standard input, bypassing the queue and Step Functions. Use the function's short name as list-lambdas prints it; the resource prefix is added for you.

cirrus manage name-dev list-lambdas
<payload.json cirrus manage name-dev invoke-lambda process

Invoking process this way runs the full intake on the payload and starts an execution, exactly as a queued message would, but the payload never touches the queue and a failure surfaces as the command's error output rather than on the dead-letter queue.

docs.title: Template payloads
docs.text:
Both templating commands substitute $-variables in a payload read from standard input, using Python's string.Template syntax with one extension: ${name?default} supplies a default when the variable is unset. cirrus payload template uses only the variables given on the command line. cirrus manage <deployment> template-payload also loads the deployment's configuration values, so a template can reference ${CIRRUS_DATA_BUCKET} and the like.

<payload-template.json cirrus payload template --var EXAMPLE_VAR value
<payload-template.json cirrus manage name-dev template-payload --var EXAMPLE_VAR value

Variables can also come from files of NAME=value lines passed as positional arguments. An unset variable without a default is an error unless --silence-templating-errors is given, in which case it is left as is.

docs.title: Validate a payload locally
docs.text:
<payload.json cirrus payload validate
<payload.json cirrus payload get-id

validate runs the same CirrusPayload.validate that process runs, and requires the payload to have an id. get-id prints the payload's id, generating one from the items and workflow name when it has none.

docs.title: Run local tools with deployment configuration
docs.text:
exec replaces the shell's process with the command; call runs it as a child and exits with its return code. Both first load the deployment's configuration values into the environment, which lets a local script or cirrus.lib session use the deployment's resources:

cirrus manage name-dev exec env | grep CIRRUS
cirrus manage name-dev call python my-script.py

docs.title: Migrate a pre-2.0 deployment
docs.text:
cirrus manage name-dev migrate --dry-run
cirrus manage name-dev migrate

See Upgrading to 2.0 for what the migration changes.
