docs.title: Using the CLI
docs.text:
The Cirrus CLI, the cirrus command, operates an existing deployment. It submits and reruns payloads, inspects executions, queries the state database, fetches stored payloads and logs, and invokes the framework's Lambda functions directly. It is part of the cirrus-geo package, built with click, and its code lives under cirrus.management.

This page covers installation, credentials, and how the CLI finds a deployment. Worked examples are in Common workflows, and every command's options are in the Command reference. Deploying Cirrus itself is Deploying to AWS.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
pipx install 'cirrus-geo[cli]'

The cli extra adds the CLI's own dependencies, click, click-option-group, and backoff, on top of the package. To run one command without installing:

uvx --from 'cirrus-geo[cli]' cirrus version

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
The CLI calls AWS through boto3, so any credential source boto3 resolves works: a named profile, environment variables, an instance role. The --profile and --region options, given before the subcommand, select a profile and region for the session:

cirrus --profile prod --region us-west-2 list-deployments

With IAM Identity Center, configure a profile once with aws configure sso and start each session with aws sso login --profile <name>. When the session has expired, the CLI reports it and exits rather than retrying.

docs.title: Required permissions
docs.text:
The identity needs permission for the AWS calls behind the commands it runs:

  • ssm:GetParameter on /cirrus/deployments/<name> and ssm:GetParametersByPath on /deployment/<name>/ for deployment discovery, and on /cirrus/deployments/ for list-deployments.
  • lambda:ListFunctions and lambda:InvokeFunction for list-lambdas and invoke-lambda.
  • sqs:SendMessage on the process queue for process and run-workflow.
  • s3:GetObject on the payload bucket to fetch payloads, and s3:PutObject to enqueue a payload larger than an SQS message.
  • dynamodb:GetItem, BatchGetItem, and Query on the state table and its indexes, plus Scan and UpdateItem for migrate.
  • states:DescribeExecution, GetExecutionHistory, and DescribeStateMachine for the get-execution* and get-workflow-definition commands.
  • logs:FilterLogEvents and logs:GetLogEvents for get-lambda-logs and get-batch-logs.

Scope the grant to the commands the identity uses.

docs.title: Assuming a role
docs.text: A deployment can name a role for the CLI to assume, either as a CIRRUS_CLI_IAM_ARN entry in its Parameter Store configuration or as cirrus manage <deployment> --iam-arn <role-arn> on the command line. The CLI calls sts:AssumeRole on that ARN with the current credentials and uses the temporary credentials, under the session name cirrus_cli_session, for every call against that deployment. The caller then needs only sts:AssumeRole on the role, and the permissions above live on the role. When both are present, the Parameter Store value wins and --iam-arn is ignored. No template creates the parameter; add it by hand when wanted.

docs.title: Deployment discovery
docs.text:
Commands under manage take a deployment name and look up that deployment's resources in Parameter Store at run time. The pointer parameter /cirrus/deployments/<name> holds a JSON value naming where the configuration lives, by default the path /deployment/<name>/. Under that path is one parameter per configuration value. The CLI requires CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_BUCKET, CIRRUS_STATE_DB, CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL, CIRRUS_BASE_WORKFLOW_ARN, and CIRRUS_PREFIX, and fails with a message naming any that are missing. The full set the templates publish is under Deployment contract: Parameter Store entries.

flowchart LR
    A["cirrus manage name-dev list-lambdas"] --> B["GetParameter\n/cirrus/deployments/name-dev"]
    B --> C["GetParametersByPath\n/deployment/name-dev/*"]
    C --> D["AWS API calls using the\nresolved configuration"]

cirrus list-deployments prints every name under /cirrus/deployments/ visible to the current credentials. cirrus manage <deployment> show prints the resolved configuration.

cloudformation/cli/ssm_parameters.yaml creates the pointer and configuration parameters as part of the main stack, with the deployment name equal to ResourcePrefix. A deployment built with other tooling needs to create the same parameters for the CLI to find it.

docs.title: Command structure
docs.text:
Deployment-scoped commands are cirrus manage <deployment> <command>. mgmt is an alias for manage, and every command group resolves any unambiguous prefix of a command name, so these are equivalent:

cirrus manage name-dev list-lambdas
cirrus mgmt name-dev list-lambdas
cirrus mgmt name-dev list-l

Commands that take a payload read it from standard input. Commands that return JSON pretty-print it by default and accept --raw to print it compact, and the bulk query commands print one JSON object per line.

docs.title: Your first pipeline
docs.text:
This adds a workflow with one Lambda task of your own to a running deployment, submits a payload through it, and reads back what happened. It works against the Quickstart deployment on LocalStack or a deployment made with Deploying to AWS; the commands are the same once the matching environment file is sourced.

The task is deliberately small. It takes the payload, stamps each item with the time it ran, and returns the payload. That is enough to show the pieces a real pipeline is built from and where each one is documented.

docs.title: 1. The task and the workflow
docs.text:
Save the following as hello-workflow.yaml. It is one CloudFormation template holding the task, as a Lambda function with its code inline, the workflow, as a Step Functions state machine, and the two roles they run under.

AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: 'Cirrus tutorial - hello workflow with one Lambda task'

Parameters:
  ResourcePrefix:
    Type: String
    Description: Prefix for all resource names
  LambdaPythonVersion:
    Type: String
    Description: Python version for the task function, for example 3.13

Resources:
  HelloTaskRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-hello-task-role'
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: lambda.amazonaws.com
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole

  HelloTask:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-hello-task'
      Runtime: !Sub 'python${LambdaPythonVersion}'
      Handler: index.handler
      Role: !GetAtt HelloTaskRole.Arn
      Timeout: 30
      Code:
        ZipFile: |
          from datetime import UTC, datetime


          def handler(payload, context):
              stamp = datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()
              for item in payload["features"]:
                  item.setdefault("properties", {})["tutorial:processed"] = stamp
              return payload

  HelloWorkflowRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      RoleName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-hello-workflow-role'
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: states.amazonaws.com
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: InvokeHelloTask
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
                Resource: !GetAtt HelloTask.Arn

  HelloWorkflow:
    Type: AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine
    Properties:
      StateMachineName: !Sub '${ResourcePrefix}-hello'
      RoleArn: !GetAtt HelloWorkflowRole.Arn
      DefinitionString: !Sub |
        {
          "Comment": "Tutorial workflow with one Lambda task",
          "StartAt": "hello-task",
          "States": {
            "hello-task": {
              "Type": "Task",
              "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
              "Parameters": {
                "FunctionName": "${HelloTask.Arn}",
                "Payload.$": "$"
              },
              "OutputPath": "$.Payload",
              "End": true,
              "Retry": [
                {
                  "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.Unknown"],
                  "IntervalSeconds": 1,
                  "BackoffRate": 2,
                  "MaxAttempts": 5
                }
              ],
              "Catch": [
                {
                  "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"],
                  "ResultPath": "$.error",
                  "Next": "failure"
                }
              ]
            },
            "failure": {
              "Type": "Fail",
              "ErrorPath": "$.error.Error",
              "CausePath": "$.error.Cause"
            }
          }
        }

Four things in it are Cirrus conventions rather than choices:

  • The state machine name, ${ResourcePrefix}-hello. process finds a workflow by prepending the prefix to the workflow name in the payload, and update-state is only invoked for state machines with that prefix. See Naming and dispatch.
  • "OutputPath": "$.Payload" on the task state. The lambda:invoke integration wraps the function's return value, and update-state needs the execution's output to be the payload itself.
  • The Catch and Fail pair. The task's error is stored under $.error and the Fail state reads it back with ErrorPath and CausePath, which is how the error reaches the state database. See Capturing errors.
  • The handler's contract: a payload in, a payload out, with features holding the output items. Everything else about the function is ordinary Lambda.

docs.title: 2. Deploy it
docs.text:
The workflow stack needs the same ResourcePrefix as the core stack, which is in the sourced environment file as RESOURCE_PREFIX:

aws cloudformation deploy \
  --template-file hello-workflow.yaml \
  --stack-name "$RESOURCE_PREFIX-hello-workflow" \
  --parameter-overrides \
    "ResourcePrefix=$RESOURCE_PREFIX" \
    "LambdaPythonVersion=$LAMBDA_PYTHON_VERSION" \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM

Nothing in the core stack changes. The only link between the two stacks is the name.

docs.title: 3. Submit a payload
docs.text:
Save this as payload.json:

{
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "id": "tutorial/workflow-hello/item-1",
    "features": [
        {
            "id": "item-1",
            "collection": "tutorial",
            "properties": {}
        }
    ],
    "process": [
        {
            "workflow": "hello"
        }
    ]
}

The id follows <collections>/workflow-<workflow>/<itemids>, and process[0].workflow is hello, the part of the state machine name after the prefix. The item is a stub with only an id and a collection, which is all Cirrus requires of an item. See Payload schema.

<payload.json cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" run-workflow

run-workflow enqueues the payload, waits for the execution to finish, and prints the output payload. The item comes back with the property the task added:

{
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "id": "tutorial/workflow-hello/item-1",
    "features": [
        {
            "id": "item-1",
            "collection": "tutorial",
            "properties": {
                "tutorial:processed": "2026-09-20T13:39:25.788603+00:00"
            }
        }
    ],
    "process": [
        {
            "workflow": "hello"
        }
    ]
}

Between those two commands, process took the payload off the queue, wrote a CLAIMED record to the state database, uploaded the payload to the payload bucket, and started the execution; the state machine invoked the function; and update-state recorded the result, stored the output payload, and published the item to the publish topic. See Life of a payload.

docs.title: 4. Read what happened
docs.text:
The state database record:

cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" get-state tutorial/workflow-hello/item-1

{
    "collections_workflow": "tutorial_hello",
    "itemids": "item-1",
    "state_updated": "SUCCEEDED_2026-09-20T13:39:25.890088+00:00",
    "updated": "2026-09-20T13:39:25.890088+00:00",
    "created": "2026-09-20T13:39:24.553341+00:00",
    "claimed_at": "2026-09-20T13:39:24.553341+00:00",
    "executions": [
        "arn:aws:states:us-east-1:000000000000:execution:cirrus-sandbox-hello:9d45818f-9d53-5cda-9eb7-43ffaf706bbe"
    ]
}

The state is the prefix of state_updated. executions holds the ARN of the one execution so far. Each field is described under State database: Fields.

The stored output payload, which is what run-workflow printed, and the execution's event history:

cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" get-output-payload tutorial/workflow-hello/item-1
cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" get-execution-events --payload-id tutorial/workflow-hello/item-1

Both resolve the payload ID to its most recent execution. The output payload is read from executions/tutorial/workflow-hello/item-1/<execution-id>/output.json in the payload bucket, and the events from Step Functions. On AWS, get-execution-events --with-log-metadata adds the Lambda request ID to the task event so get-lambda-logs can fetch that invocation's log lines; LocalStack's Step Functions emulation does not supply the request ID, so leave the flag off there.

docs.title: 5. Submit it again
docs.text:
<payload.json cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" process

Nothing runs. The record is SUCCEEDED, so process skips the payload and emits an ALREADY_SUCCEEDED workflow event; get-state shows the same executions list as before. To run it again, set replace on the process definition and submit it with process:

python3 -c 'import json; p = json.load(open("payload.json")); p["process"][0]["replace"] = True; print(json.dumps(p))' \
    | cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" process

A few seconds later, get-state lists two executions and a newer state_updated. process rather than run-workflow here because run-workflow waits only while the record is PROCESSING, and a record that is already SUCCEEDED from the first run satisfies that at once, so it prints the earlier output before the rerun starts. The rules for which states rerun are in The replace field and reruns.

docs.title: 6. Clean up
docs.text:
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name "$RESOURCE_PREFIX-hello-workflow"

The state database record and the stored payloads remain; they belong to the core stack.

docs.title: From here to a real task
docs.text: The tutorial task has no dependencies, so its code fits inline in the template. A real task usually downloads assets, runs geospatial libraries, uploads results, and is built on stac-task, which handles the payload contract, asset download and upload, and output collection assignment. That means a container image and, for long or large jobs, AWS Batch instead of Lambda. Writing a task covers those, Defining a workflow covers retries and multi-task workflows, and Feeders covers replacing the hand-written payload with code that builds payloads from new data.

docs.title: How Cirrus works
docs.text: Work moves through Cirrus as payloads. A payload is a JSON document that holds STAC Items, names the workflow to run them through, and carries configuration for the workflow as a whole and for each task in it. You write the workflows, the tasks each workflow calls, and the code that builds payloads and sends them to a queue. Cirrus takes each payload from the queue, starts the workflow it names as a Step Functions execution, and tracks the payload's state in a DynamoDB table from claim to outcome. When an execution succeeds, Cirrus also stores the output payload in S3 and publishes each output item to an SNS topic. A STAC API ingest, a feeder for another pipeline, or any subscriber of your own picks the items up there.

docs.title: The payload
docs.text:
A Cirrus Payload is a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with a process list added. Its features are the STAC Items to process. The first process entry names the workflow to run and carries that workflow's configuration: parameters shared by every task, parameters for individual tasks, and settings for how tasks upload the assets they produce. Further entries chain other workflows after this one. The schema page lists every field.

The payload's id combines the item collections, the workflow name, and the item IDs, as <collections>/workflow-<workflow>/<itemids>. The state database is keyed on it, so the same items sent to the same workflow again are a resubmission of a payload that already ran. Cirrus skips a resubmission unless the payload says to replace the earlier run.

The intent is STAC in, STAC out. Cirrus checks that the payload has the right structure, but it does not check the items themselves, and an input item needs only an id to be accepted. The output is stored and published as the last task returned it. Whether a pipeline produces STAC is up to its tasks.

docs.title: Life of a payload
docs.text:
Below is the AWS architecture of a Cirrus deployment, drawn with two workflows. The numbered steps that follow trace one payload through it, naming each component as the payload reaches it.

  1. A feeder sends the payload to the process queue. Feeders are the grey box at the top left. The diagram shows two Lambda feeders, one of them subscribed to an external data topic, and a person submitting a payload by hand. Anything that can send a message to the queue is a feeder.
  2. process takes the payload off the queue, validates it, claims it in the state database, uploads it to the payload bucket, and starts an execution of the state machine the payload's workflow name selects, with the payload as input.
  3. The state machine runs its tasks. Tasks are not drawn: they are the Lambda functions and Batch jobs inside each Step Functions box. Each task receives the payload the previous one returned. A Lambda task gets it as its event. A Batch job cannot, so pre-batch writes the payload to the payload bucket for the job to read and post-batch reads the job's result back, which is the arrow labeled Batch task payloads. A task that produces assets can upload them to the data bucket and point its items at them, the dashed arrow at the top; nothing in Cirrus requires it.
  4. When the execution ends, the EventBridge rule invokes update-state with the status, input, and output. It records SUCCEEDED, FAILED, INVALID, or ABORTED in the state database. On success it also stores the output payload in the payload bucket and publishes each output item to the publish topic. If the payload's process list has more entries, it builds the next payload and sends it back to the queue, the arrow labeled Chained workflow payloads.

The rest of the diagram is for watching the deployment. process and update-state announce each decision they make about a payload as a workflow event on the workflow event topic, and optionally to a CloudWatch log group whose metric filters turn the events into metrics. Two dead-letter queues catch what the functions could not handle: the process queue's for messages process failed on repeatedly, and update-state's for EventBridge events it could not process. The read-only api, behind API Gateway, serves the state database and the metrics over HTTP, and its root endpoint lists workflows from a catalog.json you place in the data bucket. Monitoring covers using these.

To build a task and workflow and watch a payload take this path, see Your first pipeline.

docs.title: What you build and what Cirrus provides
docs.text:
The parts of the diagram specific to your pipeline are yours to write. The rest is the framework.

You write Cirrus provides Feeders. Any code with permission to send to the process queue. Queues. The process queue, its dead-letter queue, and a dead-letter queue for update-state. Workflows. Step Functions state machines, one CloudFormation stack each. process Lambda function. Takes payloads off the queue and starts executions. Tasks. The Lambda functions and Batch jobs a workflow invokes. Each takes a payload and returns one. update-state Lambda function. Invoked by the EventBridge rule when an execution ends. Records outcomes, stores output payloads, publishes items, and continues chains. pre-batch and post-batch Lambda functions. Pass a payload into and out of a Batch job through S3. Storage. The state database, the payload bucket, and the data bucket. Topics. The publish topic and the workflow event topic. api Lambda function. Read-only HTTP access to the state database and metrics, behind API Gateway. Metrics. An optional CloudWatch log group and metric filters over workflow events.

Cirrus asks three things of a workflow. Its state machine is named ${ResourcePrefix}-<workflow>, so that process can find it and update-state is invoked when it finishes. Its Fail state carries the failing task's error forward, so the state database records why. Its final output is the payload, since that is what update-state stores and publishes. Which tasks run, in what order, and with what retries is yours to decide.

Cirrus ships CloudFormation templates, in cloudformation/, that create everything in the right-hand column. They are not required. Each function reads the resources it needs from environment variables, so a deployment built with Terraform, AWS CDK, or hand-written templates works as long as it creates the same resources and sets the same variables. The Deployment contract specifies those resources and variables. Deploying to AWS is the procedure for the shipped templates.

docs.text:

  • Building pipelines covers tasks, workflows, and feeders.
  • Using the CLI and the Python library are the two ways to work with a deployment from outside AWS.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This runs Cirrus on LocalStack in a Docker container and submits two payloads through it, one that succeeds and one that fails. It needs no AWS account. The deployment is the core stack plus one test workflow, created by the same CloudFormation templates used to deploy to AWS.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker, to run LocalStack.
  • The AWS CLI. The provisioning script is a set of aws cloudformation and aws s3 calls, and the environment file in step 1 points them at LocalStack instead of AWS.
  • uv, which the Lambda packaging script uses to build the function distribution from uv.lock.
  • A clone of the cirrus-geo repository, since the templates, scripts, and lock file live there.
  • The Cirrus CLI: pipx install 'cirrus-geo[cli]' or uv tool install 'cirrus-geo[cli]'. See Installing.

docs.title: 1. Configure and start LocalStack
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cp .env.localstack.example .env.localstack
source .env.localstack

docker compose up -d -V

.env.localstack sets the variables every later command reads. It points the AWS CLI and the Cirrus CLI at http://localhost:4566 with placeholder credentials, names the three CloudFormation stacks, sets the RESOURCE_PREFIX (cirrus-sandbox) that starts every resource name, and sets _USING_LOCALSTACK_CONFIG=true, which the provisioning script requires before it will run. Source it again in each new shell. The placeholder credentials are a guard: the provisioning script hard-codes the same values, so nothing in this guide can reach a real AWS account.

docker compose up starts LocalStack from compose.yml at the repository root. The -V flag recreates anonymous volumes instead of reusing a previous container's, so a restart with the same command begins from empty state.

docs.title: 2. Deploy
docs.text:
./bin/localstack-provision.bash bootstrap
./bin/localstack-provision.bash deploy

bootstrap creates a stack holding one S3 bucket for deployment artifacts. deploy runs three steps:

  • Builds the Lambda function distribution as a zip file, using uv and uv.lock.
  • Packages the main template, which uploads the zip and the nested stack templates to the artifacts bucket, then deploys the main stack with EnableVpc=false.
  • Deploys the minimal workflow stack from cloudformation/workflows/minimal/.

bootstrap runs once. Rerun deploy to apply template or Lambda code changes to the existing stacks.

Note

LocalStack can be left in a broken state by a failed CloudFormation apply or rollback. If a later step cannot recover, restart it with docker compose up -d -V and redeploy from bootstrap.

The main stack registers the deployment in Parameter Store under /cirrus/deployments/, which is where the Cirrus CLI looks for deployments. The CLI reaches LocalStack through the same sourced environment as the AWS CLI, so this lists cirrus-sandbox:

cirrus list-deployments

docs.title: 3. Run the test payloads
docs.text:
The minimal workflow is a single Choice state that succeeds when the payload's process[0].succeed field is true and fails otherwise. The script's test command submits one payload of each kind and checks that the first exits 0 and the second exits 10:

./bin/localstack-provision.bash test

To submit one yourself, render the workflow's payload template and pipe the result to run-workflow. payload template reads the template from stdin and substitutes each variable given with -x. run-workflow reads the rendered payload from stdin, submits it, polls the state database until the execution leaves PROCESSING, and prints the output payload:

<cloudformation/workflows/minimal/payload.json.template cirrus payload template \
    -x id_suffix "-$(uuidgen)" \
    | cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" run-workflow

The template has three variables: succeed, default true, replace, default false, and id_suffix, default empty. A unique id_suffix gives each submission a new payload ID. Set succeed to false for a failing execution, which run-workflow reports with exit code 10 and a last_error field in place of the output payload:

<cloudformation/workflows/minimal/payload.json.template cirrus payload template \
    -x id_suffix "-$(uuidgen)" \
    -x succeed false \
    | cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" run-workflow

run-workflow polls every 15 seconds by default, so expect a short wait before it returns. You can append -p 1 to the end of the command to poll every second.

Resubmitting a payload ID that already succeeded is skipped unless replace is true. See The replace field and reruns.

docs.title: 4. Look around
docs.text:
get-state prints the state database record for a payload ID. For the last payload submitted above, substitute the UUID you generated:

cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" get-state "collection/workflow-minimal/item-<uuid>"

The record holds the state, the created and updated timestamps, the ARNs of the payload's executions, and for a failed payload the last_error.

The HTTP API is reachable through LocalStack's API Gateway emulation at a LocalStack-specific URL: /restapis/<API ID>/<stage>/_user_request_/ followed by the path the API would serve in AWS. The stage is dev. Get the API ID from the main stack's outputs, then request the item list for the collection and workflow:

API_ID=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK" \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`ApiGatewayId`].OutputValue' \
  --output text)

curl "http://localhost:4566/restapis/${API_ID}/dev/_user_request_/collection/workflow-minimal/items"

The response lists the state record of every payload whose ID starts with collection/workflow-minimal. Drop the trailing /items to get counts by state instead.

Your first pipeline continues from here by adding a workflow and task of your own.

docs.title: 5. Tear down
docs.text:
./bin/localstack-provision.bash delete
./bin/localstack-provision.bash debootstrap
docker compose down

delete removes the workflow stack, empties the data and payload buckets, and removes the main stack. debootstrap empties the artifacts bucket and removes the bootstrap stack. The buckets are emptied first because CloudFormation will not delete a bucket that still holds objects.

docs.title: Deploying to AWS
docs.text: This is the procedure for deploying the CloudFormation templates in cloudformation/ to an AWS account, updating them, and removing them. What the templates create, every parameter, and what a deployment built with other tooling must provide are on Deployment contract. Concurrency and quotas are on Scaling and quotas.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The AWS CLI, with credentials that can create every resource type in the contract and named IAM roles.
  • uv, which the packaging script uses to build the Lambda distribution from uv.lock.
  • A clone of the cirrus-geo repository.
  • The Cirrus CLI, to submit a test payload at the end. See Installing.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
Stack names and parameters come from shell variables. Copy the example file, edit it, and source it:

cp .env.aws.example .env.aws
# edit .env.aws
source .env.aws
Variable Default Sets BOOTSTRAP_STACK cirrus-bootstrap Bootstrap stack name MAIN_STACK cirrus-sandbox Main stack name MINIMAL_WORKFLOW_STACK cirrus-sandbox-minimal-workflow Stack name for the minimal workflow RESOURCE_PREFIX cirrus-sandbox The ResourcePrefix parameter, from which every resource name derives LAMBDA_PYTHON_VERSION 3.13 The LambdaPythonVersion parameter and the packaging target LAMBDA_ARCH arm64 The LambdaArch parameter and the packaging target LOG_LEVEL DEBUG The LogLevel parameter ENABLE_VPC true The EnableVpc parameter VPC_CIDR, PRIVATE_SUBNET_CIDR, PUBLIC_SUBNET_CIDR 10.1.0.0/16, 10.1.10.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24 The VPC parameters, used when ENABLE_VPC is true

The parameters are described under Main stack parameters. Set ENABLE_VPC="false" unless a function must reach something only reachable from inside a VPC; the NAT gateway the VPC stack creates is billed hourly regardless of traffic. RESOURCE_PREFIX is also the deployment name the Cirrus CLI uses.

docs.title: 1. Deploy the bootstrap stack
docs.text:
The bootstrap stack creates the bucket that packaged Lambda code and nested templates are uploaded to:

aws cloudformation deploy \
  --stack-name "$BOOTSTRAP_STACK" \
  --template-file cloudformation/bootstrap/bootstrap.yaml \
  --parameter-overrides \
    "ResourcePrefix=$RESOURCE_PREFIX"

aws cloudformation deploy creates the stack or updates it if it exists. That holds for every deploy command on this page.

docs.title: 2. Package the Lambda functions
docs.text:
./bin/build-lambda-dist.py \
    -p "$LAMBDA_PYTHON_VERSION" \
    -a "$LAMBDA_ARCH" \
    -o "cloudformation/core/lambda-packages/cirrus-lambda-dist.zip"

The script creates a virtual environment for the target Python version, runs uv sync --locked against uv.lock for the target platform, and zips the resulting site-packages with the function handlers. The main stack's function resources reference that zip path.

docs.title: 3. Package and deploy the main stack
docs.text:
ARTIFACT_BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name "$BOOTSTRAP_STACK" \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`CirrusDeploymentArtifactsBucket`].OutputValue' \
  --output text)

aws cloudformation package \
  --template-file cloudformation/main.yaml \
  --s3-bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \
  --output-template-file packaged-template.yaml

aws cloudformation deploy \
  --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK" \
  --template-file packaged-template.yaml \
  --parameter-overrides \
    "ResourcePrefix=$RESOURCE_PREFIX" \
    "LambdaPythonVersion=$LAMBDA_PYTHON_VERSION" \
    "LambdaArch=$LAMBDA_ARCH" \
    "LogLevel=$LOG_LEVEL" \
    "EnableVpc=$ENABLE_VPC" \
    "VpcCidr=$VPC_CIDR" \
    "PrivateSubnetCidr=$PRIVATE_SUBNET_CIDR" \
    "PublicSubnetCidr=$PUBLIC_SUBNET_CIDR" \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM

package uploads the Lambda zip and the nested templates to the artifacts bucket and writes a template with those locations substituted. CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM is required because the stack creates named IAM roles. The deploy waits on every nested stack, which takes several minutes.

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK" \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs | sort_by(@, &Description)' \
  --output table

cirrus list-deployments
cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" show

The outputs include the bucket names, the state table, the process queue URL, the topic ARNs, the API Gateway URL, and the Parameter Store prefix. list-deployments shows RESOURCE_PREFIX once the CLI stack's parameters exist, and show prints the configuration the CLI resolved from them.

docs.title: 5. Deploy a workflow stack
docs.text:
Each workflow is its own stack, deployed after the main stack and coupled to it only by ResourcePrefix. The in-repo minimal workflow is the smallest complete one:

aws cloudformation deploy \
  --template-file cloudformation/workflows/minimal/state_machine.yaml \
  --stack-name "$MINIMAL_WORKFLOW_STACK" \
  --parameter-overrides \
    "ResourcePrefix=$RESOURCE_PREFIX" \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM

A workflow of your own deploys the same way with its own template. See Defining a workflow.

docs.title: 6. Submit a test payload
docs.text:
<cloudformation/workflows/minimal/payload.json.template cirrus payload template \
    -x id_suffix "-$(uuidgen)" \
    | cirrus manage "$RESOURCE_PREFIX" run-workflow

run-workflow exits 0 when the execution succeeds. The template's succeed variable, set with -x succeed false, drives a failing execution. See Run a workflow and wait for the result.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
• Cirrus code or templates: repeat steps 2 and 3. package uploads a new zip and deploy updates the stack in place, including the function code.
  • A workflow: repeat step 5 for that workflow's stack. Executions already running continue on the old definition.
  • Parameters: change the value in .env.aws, source it, and repeat step 3. ResourcePrefix cannot be changed in place, since every resource name derives from it; a new prefix is a new deployment.

Updating a Batch task's resources has failure modes of its own. See Updating Batch resources.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
CloudFormation will not delete a bucket with objects in it, so empty the three buckets first:

DATA_BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK" \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`CirrusDataBucket`].OutputValue' \
  --output text)

PAYLOAD_BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK" \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`CirrusPayloadBucket`].OutputValue' \
  --output text)

ARTIFACT_BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name "$BOOTSTRAP_STACK" \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`CirrusDeploymentArtifactsBucket`].OutputValue' \
  --output text)

aws s3 rm "s3://$DATA_BUCKET" --recursive
aws s3 rm "s3://$PAYLOAD_BUCKET" --recursive
aws s3 rm "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" --recursive

Then delete the stacks: every workflow stack first, then the main stack, then the bootstrap stack.

aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name "$MINIMAL_WORKFLOW_STACK"
aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name "$MINIMAL_WORKFLOW_STACK"

aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK"
aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name "$MAIN_STACK"

aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name "$BOOTSTRAP_STACK"
aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name "$BOOTSTRAP_STACK"

Deleting the main stack deletes the state table and the payload bucket, and with them the record of every execution.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: A Cirrus deployment exposes four places to look when tracking work: the state database for per-payload state, the workflow event stream for aggregate counts and alerting, the Step Functions execution for what happened inside a workflow, and CloudWatch Logs for task and function output. This page says what each one holds and how to reach it. Command syntax is in Common workflows.

docs.title: State database
docs.text:
The state database holds one record per payload ID. Three fields answer most questions. state_updated begins with the current state. last_error is present on FAILED and INVALID records. executions lists every Step Functions execution ARN attempted for the payload, most recent last.

The Cirrus CLI reads records three ways: get-state for one payload ID, query for the records matching a collections-workflow and optional state, time window, or error prefix, and get-input-payloads for the input payloads behind those records. See Check state and stored payloads and Query the state database in bulk.

The same records are readable over HTTP through the HTTP API, which also returns per-state counts for a collections-workflow.

docs.title: Workflow events
docs.text:
Every claim, start, skip, rejection, and terminal outcome is emitted as a workflow event. Three uses for an operator:

  • Alerting. Subscribe to the ${ResourcePrefix}-workflow-event SNS topic with a filter policy on the event_type message attribute, for example FAILED and INVALID only.
  • Dashboards and alarms. With the metrics stack enabled, the ${ResourcePrefix}-workflow CloudWatch namespace holds a count per event type and per workflow. A CloudWatch alarm on all_workflows_by_event with dimension event=FAILED fires on failures across the deployment.
  • Aggregate counts. The HTTP API's /stats endpoint returns daily and hourly counts by state from the same metrics.

docs.title: Step Functions executions
docs.text:
Each workflow is a Step Functions state machine named ${ResourcePrefix}-<workflow>. The AWS console's execution detail view shows the state graph, each state's input and output, and the event history.

A state database record's executions field holds the raw execution ARNs. Records returned by query, get-input-payloads, and the HTTP API pass through StateDB.dbitem_to_item, which converts each ARN to a console URL. get-state returns the raw record, so its ARNs are unconverted.

The CLI reads an execution without the console. get-execution, get-execution-input, get-execution-output, and get-execution-events each take either --arn or --payload-id, and a payload ID resolves to its most recent execution. get-execution-events --with-log-metadata adds a logMetadata object to each TaskSucceeded and TaskFailed event for Lambda and Batch tasks: the log group and Lambda request ID, or the Batch log stream name, that the task's logs are under. See Inspect an execution.

docs.title: CloudWatch logs
docs.text:
Each framework function writes to the standard Lambda log group /aws/lambda/<function-name>, where the function name is ${ResourcePrefix}-<name>:

Function Log group api /aws/lambda/${ResourcePrefix}-api process /aws/lambda/${ResourcePrefix}-process update-state /aws/lambda/${ResourcePrefix}-update-state pre-batch /aws/lambda/${ResourcePrefix}-pre-batch post-batch /aws/lambda/${ResourcePrefix}-post-batch

Lambda tasks follow the same convention under their own function names. AWS Batch jobs log to the shared /aws/batch/job log group, one stream per job attempt. The post-batch function reads the last line of that stream to reconstruct a failed job's error.

docs.title: Isolating one Lambda invocation
docs.text:
All invocations of a function write to one log group, and a reused execution environment writes several invocations to the same log stream, so the stream alone does not isolate one run. Each invocation has a unique request ID. For a task invoked through the arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke resource, Step Functions records that ID in the execution history: in SdkResponseMetadata.RequestId of a TaskSucceeded event's output, and in the requestId of a TaskFailed event's cause. get-execution-events --with-log-metadata extracts it, and get-lambda-logs filters the log group by it:

cirrus manage name-dev get-execution-events --payload-id <payload-id> --with-log-metadata
cirrus manage name-dev get-lambda-logs /aws/lambda/name-dev-my-task <request-id>

The equivalent AWS CLI call is a filter on the request ID string:

aws logs filter-log-events \
    --log-group-name /aws/lambda/name-dev-my-task \
    --filter-pattern '"<request-id>"'

Log lines written through CirrusLoggerAdapter also carry the payload id as a JSON field, which filters a task's output by payload rather than by invocation. See Structured logging.

For a Batch job, get-batch-logs <log-stream> reads the job's stream from /aws/batch/job.

docs.title: Dead-letter queues
docs.text:
cloudformation/core/base.yaml creates two dead-letter queues, both with 14-day retention. Messages arriving on either are worth an alarm.

  • ${ResourcePrefix}-process-dlq receives a process queue message after five failed receives. process raises when any message in its batch cannot be turned into a valid payload, after deleting the messages it did handle, so only the rejected messages are retried and eventually dead-lettered.
  • ${ResourcePrefix}-update-state-dlq is the dead-letter target of the EventBridge rule that invokes update-state. EventBridge retries a failed invocation for up to 30 minutes (MaximumEventAgeInSeconds: 1800 in cloudformation/core/functions.yaml) before sending the event here. An event on this queue means an execution finished but its outcome was never recorded in the state database.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text: Symptom Cause Where to look A payload submitted with process never gets a state database record process rejected it: the message failed to parse or the payload failed CirrusPayload.validate The tmp/invalid/ prefix of the payload bucket, the RECORD_EXTRACT_FAILED or NOT_A_PROCESS_PAYLOAD event, and after five receives the process dead-letter queue. See Payload bucket: Invalid payloads The same payload passes run-workflow but not process, or the reverse run-workflow validates in the shell and requires an id; process validates in the Lambda function and generates a missing id Run a workflow and wait for the result A FAILED record whose last_error says to add ErrorPath and CausePath The workflow's Fail state does not carry the task's error forward, so update-state received no cause Capturing errors Step Functions shows SUCCEEDED but the record stays PROCESSING, and the update-state dead-letter queue has a message The output was too large for the EventBridge event, so update-state raised instead of recording it Lambda functions: Parsing the event A resubmitted payload does nothing Its record is SUCCEEDED or INVALID, which process skips unless the process definition sets replace The replace field and reruns A record is FAILED with StateMachineDoesNotExist No state machine is named ${ResourcePrefix}-<workflow> for the workflow in the payload Naming and dispatch A Batch task fails with UnknownError or a message about a missing log stream post-batch could not parse an error type from the job's last log line, or the container never started Lambda functions: post-batch

docs.title: Rerunning payloads
docs.text: get-input-payloads --rerun returns each matching input payload with replace: true set on its first process definition, so process accepts it for a fresh execution from states it would otherwise skip. Which states run by default and which need replace is defined in The replace field and reruns. The resubmission loop is in Rerun failed workflows in bulk.

docs.title: Scaling and quotas
docs.text: Three settings bound how much work a deployment can run at once: the process function's reserved concurrency, which caps how fast executions start; the process queue, which orders what starts next; and, for workflows with Batch tasks, the compute environment's vCPU ceiling. Beyond those, the limits are AWS account quotas. Earth Search has processed collections of millions of items through Cirrus; at those volumes the practical ceiling was AWS account quotas, not the framework.

docs.title: Process Lambda concurrency
docs.text:
ProcessLambda in cloudformation/core/functions.yaml sets ReservedConcurrentExecutions: 16. Each invocation claims and starts executions for one SQS batch of up to ten messages (BatchSize: 10 on ProcessLambdaEventSourceMapping), so this reservation caps how many executions can be started concurrently. It does not limit how many Step Functions executions run once started.

Raise it by editing ReservedConcurrentExecutions and redeploying. Reserved concurrency is subtracted from the account's regional Lambda concurrency pool, so weigh it against everything else running in the account.

docs.title: Process queue priority
docs.text:
core/base.yaml creates one process queue. The event source mapping consumes it in arrival order under the shared 16-way concurrency, so a large backfill can queue thousands of payloads ahead of newly arriving ones and delay them.

One remedy is a second queue for bulk work. Define it with its own dead-letter queue, mirroring ProcessQueue and ProcessDeadLetterQueue, and add a second event source mapping on process with ScalingConfig.MaximumConcurrency set on both mappings so that together they stay within the reservation:

# Illustrative. Extends the in-repo core/functions.yaml with a second queue.
ProcessLambdaEventSourceMapping:
  Type: AWS::Lambda::EventSourceMapping
  Properties:
    EventSourceArn: !Ref ProcessQueueArn
    FunctionName: !Ref ProcessLambda
    BatchSize: 10
    ScalingConfig:
      MaximumConcurrency: 12

ProcessLambdaBulkEventSourceMapping:
  Type: AWS::Lambda::EventSourceMapping
  Properties:
    EventSourceArn: !GetAtt ProcessBulkQueue.Arn
    FunctionName: !Ref ProcessLambda
    BatchSize: 10
    ScalingConfig:
      MaximumConcurrency: 4

The in-repo mapping sets no ScalingConfig, so today it draws on the full reservation. No Cirrus code reads a bulk-queue variable: CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL stays the single queue that update-state chains into and that cirrus manage ... process submits to. Routing to the bulk queue is the producer's choice. Point backfill feeders at its URL directly. process handles messages from either queue identically.

docs.title: Batch compute environments
docs.text: A workflow with Batch tasks is bounded by its compute environment rather than by Lambda concurrency. MaxvCpus is the ceiling on vCPUs allocated across in-flight jobs, and therefore on concurrent jobs, and MinvCpus keeps capacity warm between bursts at the cost of paying for it while idle. See Compute environment.

docs.title: AWS service quotas and limits
docs.text: Quotas are adjustable through a service quota increase request. Limits are not. The values below are AWS defaults at the time of writing; check the linked AWS pages before relying on them.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text:
• Lambda concurrent executions is a regional pool shared by every function in the account. Reserving 16 for process removes 16 from that pool. Size the account quota for the deployment's expected parallel volume. See AWS Lambda quotas.
  • Step Functions open executions is 1,000,000 per account per region for Standard workflows, which Cirrus state machines are. If item volume approaches this, throttle ingress at the feeder rather than raising the quota. See Step Functions service quotas.
  • Step Functions API throttling applies per account per region with a token bucket per action. StartExecution, called by process, and GetExecutionHistory, called by get-execution-events, are both adjustable. See the same page.
  • EC2 Spot vCPUs are quota-limited per instance family, with low defaults that grow with usage. Request an increase before a large Batch run on Spot. See Amazon EC2 service quotas.
  • S3 general purpose buckets default to 10,000 per account, adjustable to 1,000,000. See Amazon S3 quotas.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Lambda execution timeout is 15 minutes and cannot be raised. Longer processing runs as a Batch task. See Lambda or Batch.
  • Batch SubmitJob and DescribeJobs are limited to 50 requests per second per account per region. A burst of Batch submissions needs a Retry on Batch.AWSBatchException, as shown in Batch tasks in a workflow. See AWS Batch service quotas.

docs.title: Updating Batch resources
docs.text:
Changing a Batch task's resources in a deployment that is processing jobs has failure modes that a first deploy does not. This page covers them and two update strategies. Declaring the resources themselves is on Batch infrastructure; the core stack's own update procedure is on Deploying to AWS.

Several CloudFormation update behaviors around Batch resources can disrupt in-flight or newly-started workflow executions. None of them are Cirrus-specific; they follow from how CloudFormation and AWS Batch handle updates to these resource types.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
Executions started mid-deployment can reference a stale job definition. A Step Functions state machine calling SubmitJob (through a !Sub reference to the job definition resource) resolves to a specific job definition revision ARN. When CloudFormation deploys a new job definition revision, it deactivates the old revision before updating the state machine. An execution that starts a Batch task in the window between the old revision's deactivation and the state machine update fails with a reference to a deactivated revision.

A rolled-back deployment does not restore the previous job definition revision; it creates a new one. If CloudFormation errors out during deployment and rolls back a job definition update, AWS Batch does not reactivate the original revision. Instead, CloudFormation redeploys the pre-update definition as a new revision:

Job definition       A       B      A
Revision number      1   ->  2  ->  3

Revision 2 (B) deactivates revision 1 on creation; on rollback, revision 3 (A again) deactivates revision 2. The state machine, however, was never updated past its original reference to revision 1, so after this sequence it points at a deactivated revision permanently, not just for the deployment window. Fixing it requires another deployment or a manual state machine update.

Deleting a job queue kills every job on it. Removing or renaming a job queue resource in a template deletes the queue, which terminates any jobs still running or queued on it. This applies to any change that causes CloudFormation to replace the job queue resource, not only an intentional deletion.

docs.title: Choosing an update strategy
docs.text: Which of these failure modes matter, and how much, depends on uptime requirements and how continuously the pipeline runs jobs.

docs.title: Downtime unacceptable: blue/green updates
docs.text:
If jobs run continuously and any window of failed executions is unacceptable, avoid updating Batch resources in place. Instead, maintain two parallel copies of every Batch resource for a task, conventionally suffixed RevA and RevB, and alternate which copy is live:

ReprojectBatchJobRevA              ReprojectBatchJobRevB
ReprojectLaunchTemplateRevA        ReprojectLaunchTemplateRevB
ReprojectComputeEnvironmentRevA    ReprojectComputeEnvironmentRevB
ReprojectJobQueueRevA              ReprojectJobQueueRevB
ReprojectInstanceRoleRevA          ReprojectInstanceRoleRevB
ReprojectInstanceProfileRevA       ReprojectInstanceProfileRevB

Name the compute environment and job queue explicitly in each revision, so an update always targets the inactive copy rather than replacing the live one in place.

To update, say, the launch template while revision A is live:

  1. Copy ReprojectLaunchTemplateRevA to ReprojectLaunchTemplateRevB with the change applied.
  2. Copy ReprojectComputeEnvironmentRevA to ReprojectComputeEnvironmentRevB, pointing it at ReprojectLaunchTemplateRevB.
  3. Copy ReprojectJobQueueRevA to ReprojectJobQueueRevB, pointing it at ReprojectComputeEnvironmentRevB.
  4. Update the workflow's job queue reference from ReprojectJobQueueRevA to ReprojectJobQueueRevB.

CloudFormation creates the new (B) resources and updates the state machine reference in that order. If deployment fails at any point, the state machine and the A resources are untouched, and executions already running or newly started continue to use them.

Once the deployment succeeds and running A jobs have drained, remove the A resources. The next update alternates back to A. In practice, copying every resource on each update, rather than only the one that changed, keeps each revision fully self-consistent.

This strategy doubles the Batch resource count per task while a revision change is in flight; account for that against the 50-per-Region compute environment and job queue quota.

docs.title: Downtime acceptable, jobs intermittent
docs.text: If jobs run intermittently, and a failed execution during a deployment window can simply be retried, update Batch resources in place rather than maintaining two revisions. In this case, omitting ComputeEnvironmentName and job queue names avoids the replace-on-name-conflict failure mode described in Compute environment, at the cost of autogenerated names.

docs.title: Upgrading to 2.0
docs.text: Cirrus 2.0.0 reorganizes the payload bucket, renames the COMPLETED state to SUCCEEDED, renames two CLI commands, and changes several library APIs. This page covers what an existing deployment has to do. The changelog lists every change.

docs.title: Payload bucket layout
docs.text:
Payload keys now live under a root prefix, CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_ROOT_PREFIX, default cirrus. Each execution's input and output are stored at <root>/executions/<payload_id>/<execution_id>/input.json and output.json, and transient objects, meaning oversized payloads, Batch job input and output, and rejected messages, are under <root>/tmp/. See Payload bucket.

The templates gained a PayloadRootPrefix parameter, and the payload bucket a lifecycle rule expiring <root>/tmp/ after 10 days. A deployment with its own bucket needs an equivalent rule.

docs.title: COMPLETED is now SUCCEEDED
docs.text: The state database, the HTTP API, and workflow events use SUCCEEDED. The event type ALREADY_COMPLETED is now ALREADY_SUCCEEDED. Any query, alarm, or dashboard matching the string COMPLETED needs updating.

docs.title: Event field changes
docs.text:
• payload_url is now input_payload_url.
  • SUCCEEDED and ALREADY_SUCCEEDED events carry a new output_payload_url.
  • CLAIMED_PROCESSING events, and FAILED events emitted before an upload happened, carry no payload URL, since none exists yet.

See Workflow events.

docs.title: Running the migration
docs.text:
The migrate command brings an existing state database and payload bucket into the 2.0 layout:

cirrus manage <deployment> migrate --dry-run
cirrus manage <deployment> migrate

It scans the whole table on every run and processes each record that has no claimed_at field, treating one that does as already migrated. For each such record, in order:

  1. Copies the input payload from the 1.x key <payload_id>/input.json to the new execution key, when the record has an execution. A payload that was never stored at the old key, for example one submitted as a URL reference, is skipped.
  2. For a record in the legacy COMPLETED state updated within --since-days days, default 90, fetches the output from the Step Functions execution and writes it to the new output key. Executions older than Step Functions' retention are skipped.
  3. Updates the record: COMPLETED becomes SUCCEEDED, claimed_at is set from created, last_error is removed unless the state is FAILED, and outputs is removed unless the state is SUCCEEDED or COMPLETED.

Step 3 runs last so that a failure partway through leaves the record unmarked and a rerun finishes it. --dry-run prints each planned copy and update to stderr without writing. S3 objects are copied, never moved, so the 1.x keys remain until the operator deletes them.

Run migrate once after deploying 2.0.0. Until it has run, get-input-payload and get-output-payload cannot find payloads for pre-2.0 executions.

docs.title: CLI users
docs.text:
1.x command 2.0 command get-payload get-input-payload get-payloads get-input-payloads

New commands: get-output-payload, query, migrate, and the top-level cirrus version. Management commands no longer accept user variables; that support was removed in 1.0.0 and only the help text had kept advertising it.

docs.title: Library consumers
docs.text:
Code importing cirrus.lib or cirrus.management should review these changes.

cirrus.lib.statedb. StateDB.get_dbitem raises PayloadNotFoundError instead of returning None. set_completed is now set_succeeded. dbitem_to_item is an instance method, not a classmethod. payload_id_to_url, payload_key_to_url, and payload_id_to_bucket_key are removed in favor of payload_id_to_input_payload_url and payload_id_to_output_payload_url. The module-level get_payload_bucket and get_state_db are removed. The converted record's catalog field is now input_payload_url, and output_payload_url and claimed_at are new. See State database: Fields.

Payload bucket access. PayloadBucket in cirrus.lib.payload_bucket is the one entry point for S3 payload keys. PayloadManager.upload_to_s3 is removed.

Exceptions. PayloadNotFoundError moved from cirrus.management.exceptions to cirrus.exceptions. NoExecutionsError is removed, replaced by ExecutionNotFoundError in cirrus.exceptions. NoPayloadUrlError is new in cirrus.management.exceptions and UndefinedPayloadBucketError in cirrus.lib.errors. See Errors and exceptions.

cirrus.management.deployment.Deployment. yield_payloads is replaced by yield_workflow_items, which yields state records, and yield_input_payloads, which resolves them to payloads and takes the rerun flag. get_execution_arn takes only a positional payload_id. fetch_payload takes a direction of "input" or "output" instead of rerun. enqueue_payload accepts a dict, str, bytes, or binary file object.

docs.title: Deployment contract
docs.text:
A Cirrus deployment is a set of AWS resources plus the configuration that connects them. This page states that set as requirements: what must exist, what it must be named, and what each function must be told. The CloudFormation templates in cloudformation/ satisfy every requirement here and are the source for each statement. A deployment built with other tooling, such as the Terraform modules listed at the end, has to satisfy them the same way.

Procedures for the reference templates are on Deploying to AWS.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
The main stack, cloudformation/main.yaml, creates six nested stacks. A separate bootstrap stack, bootstrap/bootstrap.yaml, creates the artifacts bucket that aws cloudformation package uploads code and templates to before the main stack exists.

Nested stack Template Creates Base core/base.yaml Data and payload S3 buckets, the DynamoDB state table, the process SQS queue with its dead-letter queue, a second dead-letter queue for update-state, and the publish and workflow-event SNS topics VPC, optional core/vpc.yaml A VPC with one public and one private subnet, an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, and S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints Metrics, optional core/metrics.yaml The workflow-event log group and its two metric filters. See Workflow events Functions core/functions.yaml The five Lambda functions with their IAM roles, the SQS event source mapping for process, the EventBridge rule that invokes update-state, and a security group when the VPC is enabled API core/api.yaml An edge-optimized REST API Gateway proxying GET requests to the api function, deployed to a stage named dev, with access logging CLI cli/ssm_parameters.yaml The Parameter Store entries the Cirrus CLI reads. See Parameter Store entries

Only the base and functions stacks are required for payloads to flow. The API stack serves the read-only HTTP API, the CLI stack makes the deployment visible to the Cirrus CLI, and the VPC and metrics stacks are optional in the templates themselves.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Every name derives from one prefix, ResourcePrefix in the templates. Two of them are load-bearing: the state machine name prefix is how process finds a workflow and how the EventBridge rule recognizes one, and the Lambda function prefix is how the CLI lists a deployment's functions.

Resource Name Data bucket ${ResourcePrefix}-data-<account-id> Payload bucket ${ResourcePrefix}-payload-<account-id> Artifacts bucket ${ResourcePrefix}-deployment-artifacts-<account-id> State table ${ResourcePrefix}-state Process queue and its dead-letter queue ${ResourcePrefix}-process, ${ResourcePrefix}-process-dlq update-state dead-letter queue ${ResourcePrefix}-update-state-dlq Publish and workflow-event topics ${ResourcePrefix}-publish, ${ResourcePrefix}-workflow-event Lambda functions ${ResourcePrefix}-api, -process, -update-state, -pre-batch, -post-batch Workflow state machines ${ResourcePrefix}-<workflow>, one per workflow, in their own stacks Metrics log group and namespace ${ResourcePrefix}-workflow-event-metrics, ${ResourcePrefix}-workflow

The prefix is 2 to 22 characters, starts with a letter, and contains only letters, digits, and hyphens.

docs.title: Resource properties the code depends on
docs.text:
• State table keys: partition key collections_workflow, sort key itemids, both strings, with two global secondary indexes named state_updated and updated that share the partition key and sort on the attribute of the same name, projecting all attributes. See State database: Key schema.
  • Process queue: process is its only consumer, through an event source mapping with a batch size of 10. The templates set a visibility timeout of 180 seconds and redrive to the dead-letter queue after 5 receives.
  • Payload bucket: a lifecycle rule expiring <PayloadRootPrefix>/tmp/ after 10 days. See Payload bucket: Lifecycle and retention.
  • EventBridge rule: matches detail-type Step Functions Execution Status Change from source aws.states, with detail.stateMachineArn beginning arn:aws:states:<region>:<account>:stateMachine:${ResourcePrefix}- and detail.status in SUCCEEDED, FAILED, ABORTED, TIMED_OUT. Its target is update-state, with the update-state dead-letter queue as dead-letter target and a maximum event age of 1800 seconds.
  • Lambda functions: Python runtime, handlers api.lambda_handler, process.lambda_handler, update_state.lambda_handler, pre_batch.lambda_handler, post_batch.lambda_handler from the packaged distribution. The templates use a 15-second timeout, 256 MB, and reserve 16 concurrent executions for process. See Scaling and quotas.

docs.title: Main stack parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description ResourcePrefix cirrus-sandbox Prefix for every resource name LambdaPythonVersion none, required Python runtime version for the Lambda functions, for example 3.13 LambdaArch none, required CPU architecture for the Lambda functions, arm64 or x86_64 LogLevel DEBUG Value of CIRRUS_LOG_LEVEL on every function. One of DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL EnableVpc true Create the VPC stack and attach the Lambda functions to its private subnet VpcCidr 10.1.0.0/16 VPC CIDR block. Must be a /16 inside 10.0.0.0/8 PrivateSubnetCidr 10.1.10.0/24 Private subnet CIDR block PublicSubnetCidr 10.1.1.0/24 Public subnet CIDR block EnableWorkflowMetrics true Create the metrics stack and enable event logging on process and update-state PayloadRootPrefix cirrus Root key prefix for every object Cirrus writes to the payload bucket

EnableVpc and EnableWorkflowMetrics gate the CreateVpc and CreateWorkflowMetrics conditions in main.yaml, which decide whether the corresponding nested stack exists at all.

docs.title: VPC
docs.text:
core/vpc.yaml creates a VPC with one public and one private subnet in a single availability zone, an internet gateway, a NAT gateway with an Elastic IP in the public subnet, and S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints on the private route table.

When EnableVpc is true, the functions stack attaches all five Lambda functions to the private subnet. The security group allows all inbound traffic from the VPC CIDR and all outbound traffic, and each role gets the AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole managed policy.

When it is false:

  • No VPC stack is created and the functions run without a VpcConfig.
  • The api, update-state, pre-batch, and post-batch roles get AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole instead. The process role carries AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole either way.
  • The VpcId, PrivateSubnetIds, PublicSubnetIds, and LambdaSecurityGroupId stack outputs are omitted.

The NAT gateway and Elastic IP are billed hourly whether or not traffic flows through them. Cirrus's own S3 and DynamoDB traffic uses the gateway endpoints and never crosses the NAT gateway, so the VPC is only needed when a function must reach a resource that is reachable only from inside one.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Cirrus code reads all configuration from CIRRUS_* environment variables. There is no configuration file. The table gives what each function must be given.

Variable Required on Read by Purpose CIRRUS_LOG_LEVEL all five, optional cirrus.lib.logging Log level for the Cirrus loggers. Defaults to DEBUG when unset CIRRUS_DATA_BUCKET api api Bucket holding the catalog.json that the API root endpoint reads. The templates also set it on process and update-state, which do not read it CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_BUCKET all five PayloadBucket Bucket for execution, oversized, batch, and invalid payloads. PayloadBucket.from_env raises when unset CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_ROOT_PREFIX all five, optional PayloadBucket Root key prefix in the payload bucket. Defaults to cirrus CIRRUS_STATE_DB api, process, update-state StateDB State table name. StateDB raises when unset CIRRUS_BASE_WORKFLOW_ARN process PayloadManagers arn:aws:states:<region>:<account>:stateMachine:${ResourcePrefix}-, which the workflow name is appended to CIRRUS_WORKFLOW_EVENT_TOPIC_ARN process, update-state, optional WorkflowEventManager Topic that workflow events are published to. Unset disables publishing CIRRUS_WORKFLOW_LOG_GROUP process, update-state, optional WorkflowMetricLogger Log group that workflow events are written to for metric extraction. Empty or unset disables it CIRRUS_WORKFLOW_METRIC_NAMESPACE api, optional WorkflowMetricReader Metrics namespace that /stats reads. Empty or unset disables it CIRRUS_PUBLISH_TOPIC_ARN update-state, optional update-state Topic that output items are published to. Unset skips publishing CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL update-state, optional update-state Queue that chained payloads are enqueued to. Unset skips chaining CIRRUS_EVENT_DB_AND_TABLE none EventDB Deprecated Timestream destination. Not set by any template. See Workflow events

docs.title: IAM grants
docs.text:
Each function has its own role in core/functions.yaml. These are the grants the code exercises.

Function Grants process s3:GetObject, ListBucket, GetBucketLocation on any bucket; s3:PutObject on the payload bucket; read and write on the state table and its indexes; sqs:ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, GetQueueUrl, GetQueueAttributes on the process queue; sns:Publish on the workflow event topic; states:StartExecution on stateMachine:${ResourcePrefix}-*; logs:CreateLogStream, PutLogEvents, DescribeLogGroups, DescribeLogStreams on the metrics log group when enabled update-state Read and write on the state table; sqs:SendMessage on the process queue; s3:GetObject and PutObject on the payload bucket; sns:Publish on the publish and workflow event topics; the same log grants as process pre-batch s3:GetObject, ListBucket, GetBucketLocation on any bucket; s3:PutObject on the payload bucket post-batch The same S3 grants as pre-batch; logs:GetLogEvents on /aws/batch/* api s3:ListBucket, GetObject, GetBucketLocation on the data bucket; dynamodb:Query, Scan, GetItem, DescribeTable on the state table and its indexes; cloudwatch:GetMetricData, GetMetricStatistics, ListMetrics when the metrics namespace is set

process and the Batch functions read from any bucket because a payload may arrive as a {"url": ...} reference to an object stored elsewhere. Each workflow's state machine role is the workflow author's; it must be allowed to invoke the workflow's Lambda functions and, for Batch tasks, batch:SubmitJob plus the EventBridge permissions that submitJob.sync needs.

docs.title: Parameter Store entries
docs.text:
The Cirrus CLI discovers a deployment through AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. It reads a pointer at /cirrus/deployments/<name> whose value is {"type": "parameter_store", "value": "/deployment/<name>/"}, then every parameter under that path. cli/ssm_parameters.yaml creates them with <name> equal to ResourcePrefix.

Parameter under /deployment/<name>/ Required by the CLI Value CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_BUCKET yes Payload bucket name CIRRUS_STATE_DB yes State table name CIRRUS_PROCESS_QUEUE_URL yes Process queue URL CIRRUS_BASE_WORKFLOW_ARN yes The state machine ARN prefix, as on the functions CIRRUS_PREFIX yes ${ResourcePrefix}-, with the trailing hyphen, used to list and invoke the deployment's Lambda functions CIRRUS_DATA_BUCKET, CIRRUS_PUBLISH_TOPIC_ARN, CIRRUS_WORKFLOW_EVENT_TOPIC_ARN, CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_ROOT_PREFIX, CIRRUS_LOG_LEVEL no Same values as on the functions, loaded into the environment by exec, call, and template-payload CIRRUS_CLI_IAM_ARN no A role for the CLI to assume. Not created by any template. See Assuming a role

The CLI fails with a message naming the missing entries if any required one is absent.

docs.title: Other tooling
docs.text: Two Terraform alternatives to the CloudFormation templates are maintained by Element 84 in their own repositories. The FilmDrop AWS Terraform modules include a Cirrus module within a larger FilmDrop deployment. terraform-aws-cirrus-processing deploys pipeline components, meaning feeders, Batch compute environments, workflows, and tasks, on top of an existing Cirrus deployment.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text: The api Lambda function serves a read-only HTTP API over the state database and workflow event metrics. cloudformation/core/api.yaml fronts it with an Amazon API Gateway REST API. There is no Lambda function URL. All handler logic is in src/cirrus/lambda_functions/api.py.

docs.title: URL structure
docs.text:
The REST API has a GET method on the root resource and a GET method on a {proxy+} resource, both integrated with the function as AWS_PROXY. It is deployed to a single stage named dev, so the invoke URL is:

https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com/dev/<path>

Both core/api.yaml and main.yaml expose the invoke URL and API ID as the ApiGatewayUrl and ApiGatewayId outputs. Authorization is NONE on both methods, so the API is unauthenticated. API Gateway rejects any verb other than GET before the function is invoked.

docs.title: Path handling
docs.text: lambda_handler splits the request path on /, drops empty segments, and drops a leading segment equal to the stage name. The remaining segments are rejoined with / and matched against the routes below. Paths in this page are written as they appear after the stage.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Every route responds to GET with a JSON body. Every response, including errors, carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

Path Returns / A catalog-like root with links to each collections-workflow summary /stats Aggregate workflow-event counts by state: daily, hourly, and rolling hour /<collections>/workflow-<workflow> Per-state record counts for one collections-workflow /<collections>/workflow-<workflow>/items A page of state database records for one collections-workflow /<collections>/workflow-<workflow>/<itemids> The state database record for one payload ID

Dispatch is a sequence of checks on the rejoined path rather than a router:

  1. An empty path is the root.
  2. stats is the stats route.
  3. A path without the substring /workflow- returns 400.
  4. Anything else is parsed by StateDB.payload_id_to_key, which splits on /workflow- and then splits the remainder on its first /. An empty item-ID part is the summary route, the literal items is the page route, and any other value is looked up as a payload ID.

Because the page route is selected by the literal string items, a payload whose item-ID segment is exactly items cannot be fetched through the single-record route.

docs.title: Query parameters
docs.text:
Parsed once per request and applied to the summary and page routes.

Parameter Applies to Default Notes state summary, page unfiltered One of PROCESSING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, INVALID, ABORTED, CLAIMED since summary, page unfiltered Look-back window: an integer immediately followed by d, h, or m, for example 10d. Any other form raises an unhandled ValueError limit summary, page 100000 Cast with int(). A non-integer raises an unhandled ValueError. On the summary route, a count above limit is reported as the string "<limit>+" nextkey page none The payload_id of the last record in the previous page sort_ascending page 0 Parsed as bool(int(...)). 1 sorts ascending sort_index page updated Passed to StateDB.query. default uses the table's primary key, sorted by item IDs, instead of an index

Unrecognized parameters are ignored.

docs.title: Root
docs.text:
get_root reads s3://<CIRRUS_DATA_BUCKET>/catalog.json, which Cirrus does not create, and returns:

  • id: the catalog's id with -state-api appended.
  • description: the catalog's description followed by a space and State API.
  • links: a self link to the API root, one child link per entry under the catalog's cirrus.workflows object, titled <collections> - <workflow> and pointing at /<collections>/workflow-<workflow>, and a stac link to the catalog.json object.

The root URL is built from the request's domainName and path. If API Gateway supplies no domainName, root_url is None and get_root raises a TypeError from urljoin.

Example response, illustrative values
{
  "id": "my-deployment-state-api",
  "description": "My Deployment State API",
  "links": [
    {"title": "home", "rel": "self", "type": "application/json", "href": "https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com/dev/"},
    {"title": "sentinel2 - publish", "rel": "child", "type": "application/json", "href": "https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com/dev/sentinel2/workflow-publish"},
    {"title": "STAC", "rel": "stac", "type": "application/json", "href": "s3://my-data-bucket/catalog.json"}
  ]
}

docs.title: /stats
docs.text:
get_stats returns counts grouped by state under state_transitions:

  • daily: one entry per day over the last 60 days.
  • hourly: one entry per hour over the last 36 hours.
  • hourly_rolling: the current partial hour and the previous hour, queried separately and concatenated.

Each entry has the shape {"period": <str>, "interval": "day" | "hour", "states": [{"state": <str>, "unique_count": <int>, "count": <int>}, ...]}.

The source is CloudWatch metrics when CIRRUS_WORKFLOW_METRIC_NAMESPACE is set, which a default main-stack deployment does. Counts come from WorkflowMetricReader, reshaped by filter_for_dashboard: the CLAIMED_PROCESSING and STARTED_PROCESSING event types are reported as CLAIMED and PROCESSING, and event types that are not state names, such as ALREADY_PROCESSING, are dropped. On this path unique_count equals count. When the namespace is unset, the function falls back to the deprecated Timestream event database, and when neither is configured it returns:

/stats with no metrics source
{
  "error": "Endpoint /stats is not enabled because timeseries database is not configured"
}

with status 404. See Workflow events.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
/<collections>/workflow-<workflow> splits the partition key on its last underscore and returns one count per state:

Example response, illustrative values
{
  "collections": "sentinel2",
  "workflow": "publish",
  "counts": {
    "PROCESSING": 0,
    "SUCCEEDED": 1024,
    "FAILED": 3,
    "INVALID": 1,
    "ABORTED": 0,
    "CLAIMED": 0
  }
}

Each count comes from StateDB.get_counts over the state_updated index, honoring since and limit. The sort parameters do not apply.

docs.title: Items page
docs.text:
/<collections>/workflow-<workflow>/items returns {"items": [...], "nextkey": "<payload_id>"}. The page comes from StateDB.get_items_page, filtered by state and since and paged by limit, nextkey, sort_ascending, and sort_index. Each record is converted by StateDB.dbitem_to_item and then to_current, so it has the fields listed under State database: Fields plus the legacy catid and catalog aliases.

When more records remain, the response also carries nextkey, the payload_id to pass as the nextkey query parameter of the next request. Its absence means the last page.

docs.title: Single record
docs.text: /<collections>/workflow-<workflow>/<itemids> returns the record for that payload ID in the same shape as one entry of the items page.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Condition Result Path is not empty, not stats, and lacks /workflow- 400 with the plain string "<path> not found", where <path> is the request context path /stats with no metrics source configured 404 with the JSON error above Payload ID not found on the single-record route Unhandled PayloadNotFoundError. A Lambda invocation error, not a JSON response Malformed since Unhandled ValueError Non-integer limit Unhandled ValueError

Any path containing /workflow- is assumed to parse into a valid key. There is no 404 for a well-formed but unknown collections-workflow; the summary route returns zero counts.

docs.title: Data sources and permissions
docs.text:
Source Used for Configuration State table Summary, page, and single-record routes CIRRUS_STATE_DB. The role grants dynamodb:Query, Scan, GetItem, and DescribeTable on the table and its indexes Data bucket Root route CIRRUS_DATA_BUCKET. The role grants s3:ListBucket, GetObject, and GetBucketLocation Payload bucket The input_payload_url and output_payload_url fields on records CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_BUCKET and CIRRUS_PAYLOAD_ROOT_PREFIX. The URLs are constructed, not read, so no S3 permission on this bucket is needed CloudWatch metrics /stats CIRRUS_WORKFLOW_METRIC_NAMESPACE. cloudwatch:GetMetricData, GetMetricStatistics, and ListMetrics are granted only when the namespace is non-empty Timestream /stats fallback, deprecated CIRRUS_EVENT_DB_AND_TABLE. Not set by any template

The function runs with a 15-second timeout and 256 MB of memory. It reads state and never writes it.

docs.title: Lambda functions
docs.text:
Five Lambda functions ship with the core stack. They move payloads into and out of workflows, record state, and serve state over HTTP. cloudformation/core/functions.yaml creates each one as ${ResourcePrefix}-<name> with a 15-second timeout and 256 MB of memory, from the handlers in src/cirrus/lambda_functions/.

Function Trigger Role in the pipeline process The process SQS queue Turns a queued payload into a Step Functions execution and records it as PROCESSING update-state An EventBridge rule on execution status changes Records the terminal state, publishes output items, enqueues chained payloads pre-batch A workflow Task state before a Batch task Uploads the payload to S3 so a Batch job can read it post-batch A workflow Task state after a Batch task Returns the job's output payload to the state machine, or surfaces its error api API Gateway Read-only HTTP access to the state database and event metrics

docs.title: Queue trigger
docs.text: An AWS::Lambda::EventSourceMapping delivers messages from the process queue in batches of up to ten. Anything that can send to that queue starts processing: a feeder, the Cirrus CLI's process and run-workflow commands, and update-state when it enqueues the next payload in a chain. One message carries one payload.

docs.title: Intake
docs.text:
For each record in the event, lambda_handler does the following, with the helpers named in cirrus.lib.utils.
